subtopics.title: Embedded Systems Overview & Classification
subtopics.subtitle: What makes a system embedded, competing design metrics, and how embedded systems are classified

concepts.text: What an Embedded System Is

An embedded system is a microprocessor-based computing system designed to perform a specific, dedicated task, usually as part of a larger product and often under strict real-time, size, cost and power constraints. Vahid and Givargis define it loosely as any computing system other than a desktop computer: the processor inside a washing machine, a car engine controller, a pacemaker or a router is embedded, while the user never sees a general-purpose computer. Billions of such systems are manufactured every year, far more than desktop machines.
Three characteristics shared by almost all embedded systems:
items: Single-functioned: the system executes one program, or a small fixed set of programs, repeatedly for the life of the product (a pager always runs the pager program), unlike a PC that runs whatever the user installs.
Tightly constrained: design metrics such as cost, size, performance and power have hard limits. A remote control must be cheap, fit in the hand, respond instantly and run for a year on batteries.

Reactive and real-time: the system continually responds to changes in its environment (sensor inputs, network packets) and must compute results within fixed deadlines; a late result from a car brake controller is as bad as a wrong one.

concepts.text: Typical building blocks of an embedded system:
items: Core processor: a microcontroller (AVR/Arduino, ARM Cortex-M, PIC, 8051), a DSP or a system-on-chip; sometimes custom hardware in an ASIC or FPGA.
Memory: Flash or ROM for the fixed program, RAM (SRAM) for variables and buffers, sometimes EEPROM for calibration data.
I/O interfaces: GPIO pins, ADC and DAC for analog signals, PWM outputs for motors and LEDs, timers and watchdog.
Communication modules: UART, SPI, I2C on the board; CAN, USB, Ethernet, Wi-Fi or Bluetooth to the outside world.
Sensors and actuators, a power supply or battery management, and firmware that may run bare-metal or on a real-time operating system.

concepts.text: Design Metrics and Their Trade-offs
Common design metrics (a measurable feature of an implementation):
items: NRE (non-recurring engineering) cost: the one-time cost of designing the system; paid once regardless of how many units are made.
Unit cost: the money spent to manufacture each copy, excluding NRE.
Size: physical space, measured in bytes for software and in gates or transistors for hardware.
Performance: execution time or throughput; latency (time from start to finish of a task) and throughput (tasks per unit time) can differ.
Power: energy consumed per unit time, which decides battery life, heat and cooling.
Flexibility: how cheaply the functionality can be changed without large NRE cost.
Time-to-prototype: time to build a working version; time-to-market: time until the product can be sold.
Maintainability, correctness (does it do what was specified) and safety (does it never cause harm).

concepts.text: These metrics compete: shrinking size may raise power, adding custom hardware improves performance and power but increases NRE cost and destroys flexibility, and a faster clock raises power. Improving one metric usually worsens another, so the designer must understand both hardware and software and pick the implementation that best balances the metrics for the intended production volume. Because NRE is spread over every unit sold, a high-NRE custom design is only economical at high volume.

Time-to-market matters because product revenue follows a rough triangle: sales rise after launch, peak in the middle of the market window and fall to zero after 2W months. A product launched D months late enters a smaller triangle and, by the simplified revenue model, loses the fraction D(3W minus D) / (2W squared) of total revenue. With a one-year window (W = 26 weeks) a delay of only 4 weeks costs about 22 percent of revenue, so a late but perfect product can earn less than an earlier, adequate one.

concepts.plainText: Percentage revenue loss = D(3W - D) / (2 W^2), D = delay, 2W = market window

concepts.text: Classification of Embedded Systems
Classification by function and operating context:
items: Stand-alone: works independently, takes inputs from sensors or keys and drives outputs directly; digital camera, microwave oven, MP3 player.

Real-time: must produce results within a deadline. Hard real-time means a missed deadline is a system failure (airbag, flight control, pacemaker); soft real-time tolerates occasional misses with degraded quality (video streaming, DVD player).
Networked: connected to a LAN, WAN or the Internet and often acting as a client or server; home security system, IoT sensor node, network printer.
Mobile: portable and battery powered with tight size, weight and energy limits; mobile phones, smart watches, handheld GPS units.

concepts.text: Classification by complexity and by processor type:
items: Small-scale: a single 8-bit or 16-bit microcontroller, little memory, programmed in C or assembly, no operating system (toys, simple appliances).
Medium-scale: one or more 16/32-bit microcontrollers or DSPs, more memory, an RTOS and complex software tools (routers, printers).
Sophisticated: 32/64-bit processors, systems-on-chip, FPGA or ASIC co-processors and an embedded Linux or RTOS with heavy hardware-software co-design (mobile phones, automotive ECUs).
By processor type the three choices are general-purpose, single-purpose and application-specific instruction-set processors, compared in the table below.

rows: Medium to high; needs compiler and tools

concepts.text: Three technologies the embedded designer chooses among (Moore's law, transistor counts doubling every 18 months, keeps pushing all three):
items: Processor technology: general-purpose (software), single-purpose (hardware) or ASIP; the architecture used to implement the desired functionality.

IC technology: how the processor is mapped onto silicon: full-custom VLSI, semi-custom ASIC (gate array or standard cell) or programmable logic device (PLD, FPGA); higher NRE buys lower unit cost, size and power.

Design technology: the tools that convert the concept into an implementation: compilation and synthesis, libraries and IP cores, test and verification; better tools shrink NRE cost and time-to-market.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Cost Models, Market Windows and Technology Choices

The simplified time-to-market model draws revenue against time as a triangle. An on-time product's revenue rises linearly from launch at time 0 to a peak at W and falls back to zero at 2W, so with a rise of one unit per unit time its area is (1/2)(2W)(W) = W². A product launched D late climbs at the same rate, must peak at the same time W because the market does not wait for it, and still dies at 2W, so its triangle has base 2W − D and height W − D. The fraction of revenue lost is the difference of the two areas divided by W², which simplifies to D(3W − D)/(2W²).

concepts.plainText: Loss fraction = [W^2 − (1/2)(2W − D)(W − D)] / W^2 = D(3W − D) / (2W^2); 2W = market window, D = delay

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: revenue lost by a late launch
Market window 2W = 20 months (W = 10); on-time revenue $8.0 million
Delay D = 3 months
Loss = D(3W - D) / (2W^2) = 3 x (30 - 3) / (2 x 100) = 81 / 200 = 0.405
Revenue lost = 0.405 x $8.0 million = $3.24 million (naive 3/20 = 15 % is far too low)
Largest delay for a loss of at most 20 %:  D(30 - D) <= 0.20 x 200 = 40
D^2 - 30D + 40 >= 0  ->  D <= (30 - sqrt(900 - 160)) / 2 = (30 - 27.20) / 2
D <= 1.40 months: about six weeks late already costs a fifth of the revenue

Total cost = NRE + unit cost × N and per-product cost = NRE/N + unit cost, where N is the production volume. For two technologies where NRE1 is lower than NRE2 but unit cost u1 is higher than u2, the total costs are equal at the break-even volume N_be = (NRE2 − NRE1)/(u1 − u2); below N_be the low-NRE choice is cheaper and above it the low-unit-cost choice wins. As N grows the per-product cost falls towards the unit cost, which is why full-custom or standard-cell silicon pays off only for high-volume products, while FPGAs and off-the-shelf processors suit small runs.

concepts.plainText: Break-even volume N_be = (NRE2 − NRE1) / (u1 − u2), where u1 and u2 are the unit costs and NRE1 < NRE2

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: choosing among three technologies
Option             NRE        Unit cost
A  FPGA            $5,000     $40
B  gate array      $45,000    $15
C  standard cell   $250,000   $5
A = B at (45,000 - 5,000) / (40 - 15)    = 1,600 units
B = C at (250,000 - 45,000) / (15 - 5)   = 20,500 units
Cheapest: A below 1,600 units, B from 1,600 to 20,500, C above 20,500
At N = 10,000: A $405,000 ($40.50 each), B $195,000 ($19.50), C $300,000 ($30.00)

concepts.text: Design technology and designer productivity:
items: Compilation and synthesis automate the move down the abstraction levels: behavioural (high-level) synthesis turns a sequential program into a datapath and controller, RT synthesis turns FSMs and register transfers into gates and flip-flops, logic synthesis optimises the gate network, and a compiler turns C into machine code.
Libraries and IP cores bring in pre-designed, pre-verified blocks such as a UART, a USB controller or a whole processor core, so they need not be designed again.
Test and verification (simulation, co-simulation of hardware and software, formal checks, FPGA prototypes) catch errors at each level and avoid costly iterations late in the flow.

Productivity gap: IC capacity has grown about 58 % per year while designer productivity grew about 21 % per year (SEMATECH figures quoted by Vahid), so the transistors available outrun what teams can design.
Mythical man-month: adding designers adds communication overhead; beyond some team size each extra person lowers total output and the project finishes later.

rows: Microwave oven; flight control; IP camera; smart watch
Hard (failure), firm (late result useless but harmless), soft (quality degrades)
Airbag; a sensor reading discarded when late; video player
Event-triggered (interrupts on input changes) or time-triggered (fixed timer ticks)
Keypad controller; engine ECU sampling every 5 ms
Reactive (continuous, at the environment's pace) or transformational (input, compute, stop)

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: latency, throughput and power
Camera: one image takes 0.4 s end to end -> latency 0.4 s, throughput 2.5 images/s
Two equal pipelined stages of 0.2 s: throughput 5 images/s, latency still 0.4 s
Dynamic power P = aCV^2f; supply lowered from 5.0 V to 3.3 V, same C and f
P_new / P_old = (3.3 / 5.0)^2 = 0.4356  ->  56.4 % less dynamic power
Also halving f: P ratio = 0.4356 x 0.5 = 0.218, but the task takes twice as long
Energy per task = P x t is proportional to V^2 only: 0.4356 of the original either way

Common slips: W is half the market window, not the whole window; the loss formula gives a fraction, so multiply by 100 for a percentage and by the on-time revenue for money. Per-product cost includes NRE/N while unit cost does not, and pipelining raises throughput but does not shorten the latency of a single task.

formulas.plainText: Cost per unit = unit cost + NRE / N units
Revenue loss fraction = D(3W - D) / (2 W^2)
Dynamic power = activity factor x switched capacitance x V^2 x frequency
Moore's law: transistors per chip double about every 18 months

notes.text: Remember the three defining characteristics as one phrase: single-functioned, tightly constrained, reactive and real-time. NRE is the one-time design cost; unit cost is per copy. MCQs often swap these two definitions.

Hard versus soft real-time is about the consequence of a missed deadline, not about speed. A pacemaker running at a few hertz is hard real-time; a video player at 60 frames per second is soft real-time.

The three processor types differ only in how much of the datapath and controller is fixed: general-purpose has a general datapath and a program memory, single-purpose has a custom datapath and controller with no program memory, and an ASIP sits in between.

formulas.title: Cost per unit
formulas.plainText: Cost per unit = unit cost + NRE / N
formulas.description: Total cost of one product when the one-time NRE cost is amortised over N units; a high-NRE custom design becomes cheaper than a general-purpose one only at large N.

formulas.title: Time-to-market revenue loss
formulas.plainText: Revenue loss = D(3W - D) / (2 W^2)
formulas.description: Fraction of lifetime revenue lost by entering the market D months late when the market window lasts 2W months (simplified triangular revenue model).

formulas.title: Dynamic power
formulas.plainText: P_dyn = alpha x C x V^2 x f
formulas.description: Switching power of CMOS logic; lowering supply voltage V has the largest effect, and clock gating reduces the activity factor alpha.

formulas.title: Moore's law
formulas.plainText: Transistor count doubles roughly every 18 months
formulas.description: Empirical growth of IC transistor density that lets embedded systems pack more functionality into cheaper, smaller and lower-power chips every generation.

flashcards.front: What are the three common characteristics of embedded systems?
flashcards.back: Single-functioned (runs one dedicated program repeatedly), tightly constrained (strict cost, size, performance and power limits) and reactive/real-time (responds to its environment within deadlines).

flashcards.front: Distinguish NRE cost from unit cost.
flashcards.back: NRE (non-recurring engineering) cost is the one-time cost of designing the system; unit cost is the cost of manufacturing each additional copy. Cost per unit = unit cost + NRE / volume.

Stand-alone (works independently, e.g. microwave), real-time (hard: missed deadline is failure; soft: occasional miss tolerated), networked (LAN/Internet connected) and mobile (portable, battery powered).

flashcards.front: Name the three technologies an embedded designer chooses among.
flashcards.back: Processor technology (general-purpose, single-purpose, ASIP), IC technology (full-custom, semi-custom ASIC, PLD/FPGA) and design technology (compilation/synthesis, libraries/IP, test/verification).

questions.questionText: A product has a market window of 24 months (W = 12). Using the simplified time-to-market model, a launch delay of 3 months loses approximately what fraction of total revenue?
Which embedded-system design metric is a one-time cost that does not change with the number of units manufactured?
questions.explanation: Non-recurring engineering (NRE) cost is the monetary cost of designing the system, paid once; unit cost is paid for every copy produced.

questions.questionText: An automobile airbag controller, where a missed deadline can cause injury, is best classified as which type of embedded system?
questions.explanation: In a hard real-time system a missed deadline is a total system failure; soft real-time systems such as media players only degrade in quality when deadlines are missed.

questions.questionText: A digital camera runs the same fixed firmware for its whole life and never runs programs installed by the user. Which characteristic of embedded systems does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Vahid lists three characteristics: single-functioned (one program executed repeatedly), tightly constrained (hard limits on cost, size, power and performance) and reactive/real-time. Running one fixed program is the first.

questions.questionText: A car's cruise controller continuously reads the vehicle speed and adjusts the throttle at the pace set by the road and the driver, for as long as it is switched on. Which term describes this behaviour?
questions.explanation: A reactive system keeps interacting with its environment and must respond to changes when they occur; a transformational program reads its input, computes a result and stops.

questions.questionText: An IP security camera streams its video over the Internet to a monitoring server and can be configured from a web browser. In the functional classification of embedded systems (stand-alone, real-time, networked, mobile), which class does it belong to?
questions.explanation: A networked embedded system is connected to a LAN, WAN or the Internet and often acts as a client or server; a stand-alone system works on its own, and small-scale is a complexity class, not a functional one.

questions.questionText: Which statement about real-time embedded systems is NOT correct?
options: A late result from a hard real-time system counts as a failure even if its value is correct
A soft real-time system tolerates occasional deadline misses with degraded quality
Correctness depends on both the logical result and the time at which it is produced
A hard real-time system is one that must run at a very high clock frequency
questions.explanation: Hard versus soft is about the consequence of missing a deadline, not about speed: a pacemaker with millisecond deadlines on a slow microcontroller is hard real-time.

questions.questionText: An engine-control unit samples its sensors and runs its control tasks every 5 ms on a timer tick, regardless of when the inputs change. How is it classified by the way its processing is started?
questions.explanation: A time-triggered system acts at fixed, pre-planned instants driven by a clock; an event-triggered system acts when an interrupt signals a change such as a key press.

questions.questionText: An electronic toy is built around a single 8-bit microcontroller with a few kilobytes of memory and is programmed in C without an operating system. How does Raj Kamal classify it?
questions.explanation: Small-scale systems use one 8- or 16-bit microcontroller with little hardware and software complexity, are often battery operated, and are programmed with an editor, assembler or C compiler.

questions.questionText: A network router uses a single 32-bit RISC processor, several megabytes of memory and an RTOS, needs no hardware-software co-design, and is developed with an IDE, a simulator and a debugger. How does Raj Kamal classify it?
questions.explanation: Medium-scale systems use one or a few 16- or 32-bit microcontrollers, DSPs or RISC processors, have noticeable hardware and software complexity, and rely on an RTOS and tools such as simulators, debuggers and IDEs.

questions.questionText: Which feature marks a sophisticated embedded system in Raj Kamal's classification?
options: A single 8-bit microcontroller and no operating system
Battery operation with a few kilobytes of RAM
Enormous hardware and software complexity needing hardware-software co-design, often with configurable processors or programmable logic
Programming only in assembly language with a cross-assembler
questions.explanation: Sophisticated systems, such as smartphones or real-time video systems, combine scalable or configurable processors, FPGAs and large software stacks, and may even need tools that are not readily available.

questions.questionText: Which design metric is the time needed to build a working version of the system, possibly bigger or more expensive than the final product, in order to verify and refine its functionality?
questions.explanation: Vahid separates time-to-prototype (a working but not final version) from time-to-market (the product can be released and sold).

questions.questionText: In embedded-system design, what does the metric flexibility mean?
options: The ability to keep working when a component fails
The ability to change the system's functionality without incurring a heavy NRE cost
The number of different products that can share one circuit board
The ease of fitting the device into a small enclosure
questions.explanation: Software on a processor is flexible because new functions only need new code; a hard-wired single-purpose circuit must be redesigned and refabricated, which is costly.

questions.questionText: Which design metric describes how easily the system can be modified after its initial release, especially by designers who did not originally design it?
questions.explanation: This is Vahid's definition of maintainability. Flexibility concerns changing the functionality without a heavy NRE cost, and correctness is confidence that the functionality was implemented as specified.

questions.questionText: Which design metric expresses the probability that the system will not cause harm?
questions.explanation: Safety is about never causing harm, which is critical for pacemakers and brake controllers; correctness only asks whether the system does what was specified.

questions.questionText: How is the size design metric usually expressed for the software and the hardware parts of an embedded system?
options: Bytes for software; gates or transistors for hardware
Lines of code for hardware; gates for software
Watts for software; square millimetres for hardware
Instructions per second for software; bytes for hardware
questions.explanation: Vahid measures software size in bytes of program and data memory and hardware size in gates or transistors (or silicon area).

questions.questionText: In the performance metric of an embedded system, what is throughput?
options: The time from the start of one task to its end
The ratio of the execution times of two processors
The number of tasks completed per unit time
The time needed to build a prototype
questions.explanation: Latency is the time for one task and throughput is tasks per unit time; the ratio of execution times is speedup. Pipelining can raise throughput without reducing latency.

questions.questionText: A camera processes one image in 0.5 s from start to finish. The processing is split into two pipelined stages of 0.25 s each (ignore pipeline register delays). What are the new steady-state throughput and the latency per image?
questions.explanation: With two stages a new image can enter every 0.25 s, so throughput = 1/0.25 = 4 images/s, but each image still passes through both stages, so latency stays 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5 s.

questions.questionText: A sensor is sampled every 2 ms, and processing each sample takes 60,000 clock cycles. What is the minimum clock frequency that finishes each sample before the next one arrives?
questions.explanation: f = cycles / deadline = 60,000 / (2 × 10^-3 s) = 3 × 10^7 Hz = 30 MHz. Forgetting that 2 ms is 2 × 10^-3 s gives 30 kHz.

questions.questionText: A control loop must process 800 samples per second, each needing 25,000 clock cycles, and a design rule limits the processor load from this loop to 50 % to leave time for other tasks. What is the minimum clock frequency?
questions.explanation: Required rate = 800 × 25,000 = 2 × 10^7 cycles/s. This may be only 50 % of the clock, so f = 2 × 10^7 / 0.5 = 40 MHz; 20 MHz would load the processor fully.

questions.questionText: A CMOS microcontroller's supply voltage is lowered from 3.3 V to 1.8 V while its switched capacitance, activity and clock frequency stay the same. By about how much does its dynamic power fall?
questions.explanation: P is proportional to V², so P_new/P_old = (1.8/3.3)² = 0.298 and the power falls by about 70 %. 45 % assumes P proportional to V, and 30 % is the fraction that remains.

questions.questionText: A processor at 1.2 V and 200 MHz dissipates 150 mW of dynamic power and completes a task in 10 ms. It is switched to 0.9 V and 100 MHz; capacitance and activity are unchanged and the task needs the same number of cycles. What are the new dynamic power and the dynamic energy per task?
questions.explanation: P = 150 × (0.9/1.2)² × (100/200) = 42.2 mW. The task now takes 20 ms, so E = 42.2 mW × 20 ms = 0.84 mJ, compared with 1.5 mJ before.

questions.questionText: A battery-powered sensor node draws 30 mA when active and 0.2 mA when asleep, and it is active 10 % of the time. How long will a 1,200 mAh battery last, assuming its full capacity is usable?
questions.explanation: Average current = 0.1 × 30 + 0.9 × 0.2 = 3.18 mA, so life = 1,200 mAh / 3.18 mA = 377 h (about 15.7 days). Ignoring the sleep current gives 400 h.

questions.questionText: Replacing software running on a general-purpose processor with a custom single-purpose hardware implementation of the same function typically has which effect?
options: It improves performance and power but increases NRE cost and reduces flexibility
It reduces NRE cost and improves flexibility
It leaves all design metrics unchanged
It increases power consumption but shortens time-to-market
questions.explanation: Design metrics compete: custom hardware removes unneeded circuitry, so it is faster and more power-efficient, but it must be designed and fabricated (NRE, time) and cannot be reprogrammed.

questions.questionText: A design has an NRE cost of $50,000 and a unit cost of $12. What is the per-product cost when 10,000 units are made?
questions.explanation: Per-product cost = NRE/N + unit cost = 50,000/10,000 + 12 = 5 + 12 = $17.00.

questions.questionText: Technology A has an NRE cost of $10,000 and a unit cost of $25; technology B has an NRE cost of $70,000 and a unit cost of $10. At what production volume do the two cost the same in total, with B cheaper beyond it?
questions.explanation: 10,000 + 25N = 70,000 + 10N gives N = 60,000 / 15 = 4,000 units; above that B's lower unit cost outweighs its extra NRE.

questions.questionText: A custom chip has an NRE cost of $200,000 and a unit cost of $4. What minimum production volume brings the per-product cost down to $6 or less?
questions.explanation: 200,000/N + 4 ≤ 6 requires 200,000/N ≤ 2, so N ≥ 100,000 units. Dividing the NRE by the target price instead gives 33,333.

questions.questionText: A device sells for $50 and 8,000 units are expected to sell. Option X uses an FPGA with NRE $10,000 and unit cost $35; option Y uses an ASIC with NRE $250,000 and unit cost $15. Which option gives more profit, and by how much?
questions.explanation: Profit = N(price − unit cost) − NRE: X = 8,000 × 15 − 10,000 = $110,000 and Y = 8,000 × 35 − 250,000 = $30,000, so X is ahead by $80,000. Ignoring NRE would wrongly favour Y by $160,000; Y only wins above (250,000 − 10,000)/(35 − 15) = 12,000 units.

questions.questionText: Option A has NRE $20,000 and unit cost $50, option B has NRE $100,000 and unit cost $30, and option C has NRE $500,000 and unit cost $10. Over what range of production volumes is option B the cheapest of the three?
questions.explanation: A = B at 80,000/20 = 4,000 units and B = C at 400,000/20 = 20,000 units, so B is cheapest between them. The A = C point (12,000) does not matter because B is lower than both there.

questions.questionText: Which assumption is built into the simplified triangular revenue model used for time-to-market?
options: A late product sells for exactly as long as an on-time product, so its whole revenue curve is simply shifted later by the delay
Revenue is constant over the window, so the loss is proportional to the delay
The market window starts when the product is launched, whenever that is
A late product's revenue rises at the same rate as an on-time product's, peaks at the same time W, and the market window still ends at 2W
questions.explanation: Because the late product must peak at W and die at 2W, its triangle is both shorter and lower, which is why the loss D(3W − D)/(2W²) grows much faster than the delay itself.

questions.questionText: A product has a 20-month market window (W = 10 months) and launches 2 months late. By the triangular revenue model, what percentage of the on-time revenue does it still earn?
questions.explanation: Loss = 2 × (30 − 2) / (2 × 100) = 56/200 = 0.28, so it keeps 1 − 0.28 = 72 % of the on-time revenue. 28 % is the part lost, not the part earned.

questions.questionText: A gadget would earn $8 million over a 52-week market window if launched on time. It launches 6 weeks late. Using the triangular revenue model, how much revenue is lost?
questions.explanation: W = 26 weeks, so loss = 6 × (78 − 6) / (2 × 26²) = 432/1,352 = 0.320, and 0.320 × $8 million = $2.56 million. $5.44 million is what the product still earns.

questions.questionText: A product has a 24-month market window (W = 12 months). By the triangular revenue model, what is the longest launch delay that keeps the revenue loss at or below 25 %?
questions.explanation: D(36 − D)/288 ≤ 0.25 gives D² − 36D + 72 ≥ 0, so D ≤ 18 − √252 = 2.1 months. Using W = 24 by mistake gives 4.3 months, and 25 % of the window (6 months) assumes a linear loss.

questions.questionText: Product X has a 16-month market window and launches 1 month late; product Y has a 48-month market window and launches 3 months late. Using the triangular revenue model, which statement is correct?
options: Both lose the same fraction of revenue, 6.25 % (delay divided by window)
Y loses three times the fraction that X loses because its delay is three times longer
X loses more because its window is shorter
Both lose the same fraction of revenue, about 18.0 %
questions.explanation: The loss D(3W − D)/(2W²) depends only on D/W, which is 1/8 for both (W = 8 and W = 24). Loss = (1/8)(3 − 1/8)/2 = 0.180 for each; 6.25 % wrongly treats the loss as linear.

questions.questionText: A product would earn $2,000,000 if launched on time into a 24-month market window (W = 12 months). Design A uses an off-the-shelf processor, is ready on time and costs $600,000 in total. Design B uses a custom chip, is 2 months late and costs $350,000 in total. Treating these costs as fixed and using the triangular revenue model, which design earns more profit, and by how much?
questions.explanation: B loses 2 × (36 − 2)/288 = 23.6 % of revenue: profit = 2,000,000 × 0.764 − 350,000 = $1,177,778, against A's 2,000,000 − 600,000 = $1,400,000. A is ahead by about $222,000; ignoring the delay would wrongly favour B by $250,000.

questions.questionText: Which processor technology implements one fixed function in a custom datapath and controller and has no program memory?
questions.explanation: A single-purpose processor is a digital circuit built for one algorithm, so there is no program to store. A DSP is an ASIP: it still fetches instructions from a program memory.

questions.questionText: Which statement about processor technologies is correct?
options: A single-purpose processor gives the best performance, size and power for its one task but has high NRE cost and no flexibility
A general-purpose processor has the highest NRE cost because its datapath is designed for each product
An ASIP has no program memory, so its instructions are hard-wired
A single-purpose processor has the shortest time-to-market of the three
questions.explanation: General-purpose processors are bought off the shelf (low NRE, short time-to-market, high flexibility); ASIPs keep a program memory with a tuned datapath; single-purpose hardware trades NRE and flexibility for speed, size and power.

questions.questionText: A low-volume product must reach the market quickly and may need feature changes after release. Which processor technology is usually the best choice?
options: A single-purpose processor in full-custom VLSI
A single-purpose processor in a standard-cell ASIC
A newly designed ASIP with its own compiler
questions.explanation: An off-the-shelf processor needs almost no hardware NRE, is available immediately and can be updated by changing software; the other options need chip design time and NRE that low volume cannot repay.

questions.questionText: In which IC technology are all layers of the chip already fabricated, so that the designer implements the function by programming connections on a purchased chip?
options: Programmable logic device, such as an FPGA
questions.explanation: A PLD needs no masks at all. A gate array still needs custom metal interconnect layers, and standard-cell and full-custom designs need a full mask set.

questions.questionText: Which description fits a (masked) gate-array ASIC?
options: Every mask layer, including transistor sizes, is drawn specifically for the design
Arrays of transistors are prefabricated on the wafer and the designer specifies only the metal interconnect layers
Pre-designed logic cells are placed and routed, and all mask layers are made specifically for the design
Programmable switches on a finished chip are set by the user in the field
questions.explanation: The other descriptions are full-custom, standard-cell and FPGA respectively. Because only the wiring masks are custom, a gate array has lower NRE and a shorter turnaround than a standard-cell design.

questions.questionText: Arrange these IC technologies in order of decreasing NRE cost: full-custom, FPGA, standard-cell ASIC, gate-array ASIC.
options: Full-custom > gate array > standard cell > FPGA
Standard cell > full-custom > FPGA > gate array
Full-custom > standard cell > gate array > FPGA
FPGA > gate array > standard cell > full-custom
questions.explanation: The more layers that must be designed and masked for the product, the higher the NRE: full-custom designs everything, standard cell needs all masks from library cells, a gate array only the metal layers, and an FPGA none.

questions.questionText: Which statement about processor technology and IC technology is correct?
options: A general-purpose processor can be built only in full-custom VLSI
They are independent: a general-purpose, single-purpose or ASIP design can each be implemented in full-custom, semi-custom or PLD technology
A single-purpose processor can be implemented only on an FPGA
An ASIP must always be implemented as a gate array
questions.explanation: Vahid stresses that the two choices are orthogonal: for example a soft-core processor runs on an FPGA, while a single-purpose circuit may be a standard-cell ASIC.

questions.questionText: In Vahid's framework, what name is given to the tools and methods used to convert the designer's concept of the desired functionality into an implementation, such as compilers, synthesis tools, libraries and verification tools?
questions.explanation: Processor technology is the architecture of the computation engine, IC technology is how it is put on silicon, and design technology is how the design is carried out.

questions.questionText: A team drops a pre-designed and pre-verified UART core into its system-on-chip instead of designing one itself. Which aspect of design technology is this?
questions.explanation: Libraries and IP bring an existing implementation from a lower abstraction level into the design, saving design and verification time; synthesis would generate a new implementation.

questions.questionText: What is the name for converting a sequential program (a behavioural description) automatically into a custom datapath and controller?
questions.explanation: Behavioural synthesis produces a register-transfer design from an algorithm; logic synthesis then optimises the gate-level network, and placement and routing lay it out.

questions.questionText: As quoted by Vahid and Givargis, what does Moore's law predict about the number of transistors that can be placed on an IC?
options: It grows by about 21 % per year
It doubles every time the clock frequency doubles
questions.explanation: Vahid uses the 18-month doubling of IC capacity; about 21 % per year is the growth of designer productivity, which is what creates the productivity gap.

questions.questionText: If IC transistor capacity doubles every 18 months, by what factor does it grow in 6 years?
questions.explanation: 6 years = 72 months = 72/18 = 4 doublings, so the factor is 2^4 = 16. Four is the number of doublings, and 64 would need a doubling every 12 months.

questions.questionText: Suppose IC capacity grows 58 % per year while designer productivity grows 21 % per year. By roughly what factor does the ratio of available transistors to what a fixed-size team can design grow over 5 years?
questions.explanation: The ratio grows by 1.58/1.21 = 1.306 per year, so over 5 years (1.306)^5 = 3.8. 9.8 is capacity growth alone (1.58^5) and 2.6 is productivity growth alone (1.21^5).

questions.questionText: A 1,000,000-transistor design is to be done by a team. A designer working alone produces 5,000 transistors per month, and every additional team member lowers each designer's monthly output by 100 transistors because of communication overhead. How long does the project take with 40 designers, compared with 20 designers?
options: About 22.7 months, slower than the 16.1 months taken by 20 designers
5.0 months, twice as fast as the 10.0 months taken by 20 designers
25.0 months, slower than the 16.7 months taken by 20 designers
About 16.1 months, the same as with 20 designers
questions.explanation: With 40 designers each produces 5,000 − 39 × 100 = 1,100 transistors/month, 44,000 in total, so 1,000,000/44,000 = 22.7 months; 20 designers produce 20 × 3,100 = 62,000 per month and finish in 16.1 months. The 5.0 and 10.0 month figures ignore the overhead.

subtopics.title: Custom Single-Purpose Processor Design & Optimization
subtopics.subtitle: Logic review, FSMs, datapath + controller design from a program, the GCD example, optimizations

concepts.text: Combinational Logic Review

A single-purpose processor is a digital circuit designed to execute exactly one program: hard-wired logic with no instruction fetch, giving maximum performance and low power at the cost of zero flexibility. Because it is built directly from logic, its design starts with the basics. Transistors form gates (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR), and a combinational circuit is one whose outputs depend only on the current inputs. The standard design flow is: state the problem, build a truth table, write the output equations, minimise them with a Karnaugh map or Boolean algebra, and draw the gate-level circuit. Ready-made combinational components used in datapaths are the n-bit adder, comparator, multiplexer, decoder, shifter and ALU.
Sequential Logic and Finite-State Machines

A sequential circuit has outputs that depend on the current inputs and on the stored state; its building blocks are flip-flops, registers, counters and shift registers, all driven by a clock. Its behaviour is captured by a finite-state machine (FSM) defined by a set of states, a set of inputs, a set of outputs, a next-state function, an output function and an initial state. In a Moore machine the outputs depend only on the current state; in a Mealy machine they depend on the state and the current inputs, so a Mealy FSM often needs fewer states but its outputs can change in the middle of a clock period.
Sequential design flow (RT-level):
items: Draw the state diagram: states as circles, transitions labelled with input conditions and outputs.
Build the state table listing present state, inputs, next state and outputs.
Encode the states: n flip-flops give up to 2^n states, so the minimum register width is the ceiling of log2 of the state count.
Derive the next-state and output logic as combinational circuits using truth tables and K-maps.
Implement as a state register plus the combinational block; the clock period must exceed the longest register-to-register delay.

concepts.text: Custom Single-Purpose Processor: Datapath + Controller

Any processor, custom or general-purpose, consists of a datapath and a controller. The datapath stores and manipulates data: registers hold variables, functional units (adders, subtractors, comparators, ALUs) perform operations, and multiplexers and buses route values between them. The controller is an FSM that, in each clock cycle, reads status signals from the datapath (for example x is less than y) and sets control signals (register load enables, mux selects, ALU function) so the datapath performs the right step. In a custom single-purpose processor both blocks are built for one program, so there is no instruction register, no program memory and no decode logic.
Register-transfer level design flow from a program to a custom processor:
items: Write the desired behaviour as a program (usually in C-like pseudocode).
Convert the program to an FSMD, a finite-state machine with datapath: an FSM whose transitions may carry complex conditions and whose states carry arithmetic actions on declared variables.
Create the datapath: allocate a register for each variable, a functional unit for each arithmetic operation, and connect them with multiplexers according to the data flow.
Create the controller FSM by replacing each FSMD action with the control signals that make the datapath perform it, and each condition with a datapath status signal.
Optimise the result, then describe it in VHDL or Verilog and synthesise it.

concepts.text: Worked GCD example. The program above becomes an FSMD with roughly eight states: state 1 waits while go_i is 0; state 2 loads x from x_i; state 3 loads y from y_i; state 4 tests x != y and exits to the output state if false; state 5 tests x < y; state 6 performs y = y - x; state 7 performs x = x - y; both return to state 4; state 8 writes d_o = x and returns to state 1. The datapath needs registers x, y and d, two subtractors (or one shared), a not-equal comparator, a less-than comparator, and 2-to-1 multiplexers in front of x and y to choose between the external input and the subtractor output. The controller is the same eight-state FSM with actions replaced by control signals x_sel, y_sel, x_ld, y_ld, d_ld and conditions replaced by status signals x_neq_y and x_lt_y.
Optimizing the Custom Single-Purpose Processor
Optimising the original program (the largest gains come first):
items: Analyse the algorithm: repeated subtraction for GCD needs up to max(x, y) iterations, while the Euclidean form using a modulo operation (x = x mod y, then swap) needs only about log(max) iterations, trading a costlier operation per step for far fewer steps.
Remove redundant operations and variables, reuse computed values and choose data widths no larger than needed.
Bear in mind the hardware cost of each operation: a modulo or divide needs a large slow unit, a subtract is small, a shift is almost free.

concepts.text: Optimising the FSMD:
items: Merge states: two consecutive states with no data dependency (x = x_i and y = y_i) can be done in one state; a state whose only purpose is to test a condition can be merged with the next; constant assignments can be folded.
Separate states: an operation too slow for one cycle (a multiply) is split into several states so the clock can stay fast.
Schedule: reorder independent operations to shorten the number of cycles along the critical loop.

concepts.text: Optimising the datapath and the FSM:
items: Functional-unit sharing (allocation and binding): the two subtractors of the GCD datapath become one subtractor with multiplexers on its inputs, because y - x and x - y are never computed in the same state.
Register sharing: variables whose lifetimes do not overlap can share a register; unused multiplexers are removed.

State encoding: binary encoding uses the fewest flip-flops, one-hot uses one flip-flop per state but simpler, faster next-state logic, Gray encoding reduces switching; encoding tools search for the smallest logic.
State minimisation: merge states that are equivalent (same outputs and same next states for every input) using an implication table or partitioning.

rows: Better algorithm, fewer operations, cheaper operations
Functional-unit sharing, register sharing, mux removal, pipelining, parallel units
Pipelining, parallelism, hardware sharing, clock gating of idle registers

concepts.text: Going Deeper: From Program to Optimised GCD Processor

Vahid's conversion of a program into an FSMD is mechanical, with one template for each kind of statement. An assignment becomes one state that holds that action. A loop becomes a condition state whose true branch enters the body and whose false branch leads to a join state, and the last state of the body returns to the condition state. An if-else becomes a condition state with one path per branch, all paths ending in a join state. Applying the templates literally produces many states that do no work, which is exactly what FSMD optimisation later removes.

Worked example 1: GCD program -> FSMD with Vahid's templates
1    : while(1) test (always true)        -> 2
2    : go_i = 0 -> 2 ;  go_i = 1         -> 2-J
2-J  : join                               -> 3
3    : x = x_i                            -> 4
4    : y = y_i                            -> 5
5    : x != y -> 6 ;  x = y              -> 5-J
6    : x < y  -> 7 ;  x >= y             -> 8
7    : y = y - x -> 6-J      8 : x = x - y -> 6-J
6-J  : join -> 5             5-J : join -> 9
9    : d_o = x -> 1-J        1-J : join -> 1
Total 13 states: binary needs ceil(log2 13) = 4 flip-flops, one-hot needs 13

Optimising this FSMD removes every state that does no useful work. State 1 tests the constant 1, so it goes, and states 2 and 2-J merge into one wait state. States 3 and 4 merge because x = x_i and y = y_i do not depend on each other, and the tests x != y and x < y merge into a single three-way decision in state 5. The join states 5-J, 6-J and 1-J disappear because their transitions can be taken directly from the states before them (5-J's exit from the decision state, 6-J's return from states 7 and 8, and 1-J's return from state 9), leaving six states: wait, load, decide, y = y - x, x = x - y and output. Each loop iteration now costs 2 clock cycles instead of 4.

Worked example 2: clock cycles for x_i = 27, y_i = 12 (one state = one cycle)
(27,12) -> (15,12) -> (3,12) -> (3,9) -> (3,6) -> (3,3)    s = 5 subtractions
Unoptimised, from state 3 up to state 9 inclusive:
  states 3,4 = 2  +  s x (5, 6, 7 or 8, 6-J) = 4s  +  final 5, 5-J, 9 = 3
  cycles = 4s + 5 = 25
Optimised, from the merged load state up to the output state:
  load = 1  +  s x (5, 7 or 8) = 2s  +  final 5, 9 = 2
  cycles = 2s + 3 = 13          saving = 12 cycles (48%)

The controller is a state register plus combinational logic. Its inputs are the n_s present-state bits and the n_i status and external inputs, and its outputs are the n_s next-state bits and the n_o control signals. Written as a truth table it therefore has 2^(n_s + n_i) rows, which is also the number of words if the logic is stored in a ROM. For the unoptimised GCD controller, with 4 state bits, inputs go_i, x_neq_y and x_lt_y and outputs x_sel, y_sel, x_ld, y_ld and d_ld, that is 128 words of 9 bits; real designs minimise the table with don't-cares instead of storing it whole.

concepts.plainText: ROM bits = 2^(n_s + n_i) x (n_s + n_o); select lines of a k-input multiplexer = ceil(log2 k)

rows: Deeper next-state and output logic; several bits can toggle per transition
Simple, fast logic: each output is an OR of state bits
Most flip-flops; 8179 of the 8192 codes are unused
Only one bit changes between consecutive states, lowering switching power
Helps only when transitions follow the code sequence

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: should the two GCD subtractors be shared?
Area (gate equivalents): SUB = 40, 8-bit 2-to-1 MUX = 24
  unshared: 2 x SUB = 80          shared: SUB + 2 x MUX = 40 + 48 = 88
Delay: unshared T = tcq + tsub + tmux + tsu = 1 + 6 + 1 + 0.5 = 8.5 ns
       shared   T = 8.5 + 1 (input mux)                   = 9.5 ns
Verdict: sharing a small 8-bit subtractor costs area AND speed here;
         sharing pays off for large units such as multipliers or dividers.
Common mistakes when designing and optimising custom processors:
items: Counting one-hot flip-flops as ceil(log2 N): one-hot needs N flip-flops, binary needs ceil(log2 N).
Merging dependent assignments: in x = a + b; y = x + 1 the second statement needs the new x, but a merged state would read the old one.
Sharing one functional unit between two operations in the same state, which both need it in the same clock cycle.
Adding the delays of separate register-to-register paths: the clock period is set by the single longest path, not by their sum.
Forgetting the extra states, and therefore extra cycles, when a slow operation is separated into several states.
Treating the FSMD as the controller: the controller FSM exists only after the datapath has been built.

concepts.text: For state-count questions apply the templates literally: one state per assignment, a condition state plus a join state for each loop and each if-else. Then count flip-flops as ceil(log2 N) for binary and N for one-hot. For GCD cycle counts, first trace the operand pairs to find the number of subtractions s, then use 4s + 5 (unoptimised) or 2s + 3 (optimised).

formulas.plainText: Minimum state-register bits = ceil(log2 of number of states)
Clock period >= clock-to-Q delay + longest combinational delay + setup time
Execution time = number of controller cycles x clock period

notes.text: Moore: outputs depend on state only, so outputs are on the state circles. Mealy: outputs depend on state and inputs, so outputs are written on the transition arrows. A Mealy machine can usually do the job with fewer states.

An FSMD is not the finished controller. The controller FSM is obtained only after the datapath is built, by replacing each FSMD action with control signals and each condition with a status signal from the datapath.

Sharing a functional unit saves area but adds multiplexers and may lengthen the critical path; adding parallel units or pipelining does the reverse. Every optimisation trades one design metric against another.

formulas.title: State register width
formulas.plainText: n_FF = ceil(log2 N_states)
formulas.description: Minimum number of flip-flops in the controller state register for binary encoding; one-hot encoding instead uses N_states flip-flops.

formulas.title: Maximum clock frequency
formulas.plainText: f_max = 1 / (t_cq + t_logic,max + t_setup)
formulas.description: The clock period of a datapath or FSM must cover the slowest register-to-register path; separating a slow operation into more states shortens this path.

formulas.title: Execution time
formulas.plainText: t_exec = N_cycles x T_clk
formulas.description: Merging FSMD states reduces N_cycles while separating states allows a shorter T_clk; the product is what the user experiences.

formulas.title: States from n flip-flops
formulas.plainText: Maximum states = 2^n for an n-bit state register
formulas.description: An n-bit binary-encoded state register can represent up to 2^n distinct controller states.

flashcards.front: What are the two parts of any processor and what does each do?
flashcards.back: The datapath (registers, functional units, multiplexers and buses) stores and manipulates data; the controller (an FSM) sets control signals each cycle and reads status signals to sequence the datapath.

A finite-state machine with datapath: an FSM extended with declared variables, arithmetic actions in its states and complex conditions on its transitions; the intermediate model between a program and a custom processor.

flashcards.front: List the four levels at which a custom single-purpose processor can be optimised.
flashcards.back: The original program (better algorithm, fewer operations), the FSMD (merge or separate states), the datapath (share functional units and registers) and the FSM (state encoding and state minimisation).

flashcards.front: How is the RT-level design of a custom processor carried out from a program?
flashcards.back: Program to FSMD; FSMD to datapath by allocating a register per variable, a functional unit per operation and multiplexers for routing; then the controller FSM replaces actions with control signals and conditions with status signals.

questions.questionText: A custom controller FSM has 12 states. With binary state encoding, the minimum number of flip-flops needed for the state register is:
questions.explanation: n = ceil(log2 12) = ceil(3.58) = 4 flip-flops, which can represent up to 16 states. One-hot encoding would need 12 flip-flops.

questions.questionText: In a custom single-purpose processor, which component contains the registers, functional units and multiplexers that store and manipulate data?
questions.explanation: The datapath holds registers, functional units and muxes; the controller is an FSM that generates control signals. A custom single-purpose processor has no instruction register or program memory.

questions.questionText: In which type of finite-state machine do the outputs depend on both the current state and the current inputs?
questions.explanation: A Mealy machine's output function takes state and input, so outputs appear on transition arrows; a Moore machine's outputs depend only on the state.

questions.questionText: In a CMOS logic gate, when does a pMOS transistor conduct (act as a closed switch)?
options: When its gate input is logic 1 (high)
When its gate input is logic 0 (low)
Only while the clock is high
Only when its source and drain are both at logic 1
questions.explanation: A pMOS transistor conducts when its gate is low, while an nMOS transistor conducts when its gate is high. CMOS gates pair a pMOS pull-up network with an nMOS pull-down network so that exactly one of them conducts for each input combination.

questions.questionText: The function F(a, b, c) = a'b'c + a'bc + ab'c + abc is minimised with a Karnaugh map. What is the simplest sum-of-products form?
questions.explanation: The four minterms (1, 3, 5, 7) are exactly the cells where c = 1, so they form one group of four in which a and b both change, giving F = c.

questions.questionText: Which of the following register-transfer (RT) level components is sequential rather than combinational?
questions.explanation: A counter stores its present count in flip-flops and changes it on clock edges, so its output depends on stored state. Multiplexers, decoders and comparators have outputs that depend only on their present inputs.

questions.questionText: Which combinational component converts an n-bit binary code into 2^n output lines, exactly one of which is active?
questions.explanation: A decoder activates the single output selected by its n-bit input, for example to produce one-hot register load enables or state signals. An encoder performs the reverse mapping.

questions.questionText: In a datapath, register R can be loaded from five different sources through one multiplexer. What is the minimum number of select lines the controller must drive for that multiplexer?
questions.explanation: A k-input multiplexer needs ceil(log2 k) select lines: ceil(log2 5) = ceil(2.32) = 3. Two lines can choose among only four sources, and five lines would be a one-hot select.

questions.questionText: What does register-transfer level (RTL) design describe?
options: A circuit as registers plus the combinational operations that transform and move data between them in each clock cycle
The layout of transistors and wires on the chip
Only the Boolean equations of combinational gates, with no storage elements
The instruction set seen by an assembly-language programmer
questions.explanation: At RT level a design is expressed as registers, functional units, multiplexers and buses, and what is transferred between registers in each clock cycle, as in an FSMD. Gate-level and layout descriptions come later in the flow.

questions.questionText: Which statement about Moore and Mealy finite-state machines is NOT correct?
options: In a Moore machine the outputs are a function of the present state only
A Moore machine's outputs change as soon as an input changes, even between clock edges
A Mealy machine's outputs can respond to an input change within the same clock cycle
For the same behaviour, a Mealy machine often needs fewer states than a Moore machine
questions.explanation: Because a Moore machine's outputs depend only on the stored state, they change only after a clock edge updates the state register. It is the Mealy machine whose outputs follow input changes between clock edges.

questions.questionText: An FSM must output 1 whenever the last three input bits are 1, 0, 1, with overlapping allowed (the input 10101 gives two detections). What are the minimum numbers of states for a Mealy and for a Moore implementation?
questions.explanation: A Mealy machine needs the states 'nothing useful seen', 'seen 1' and 'seen 10', and produces the 1 on the transition that completes 101. A Moore machine needs one more state, 'seen 101', whose output is 1, giving 4.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of a custom single-purpose processor over a general-purpose processor running the same function?
options: The ability to run a different program after the product has shipped
questions.explanation: A custom single-purpose processor is hard-wired for one algorithm, so it can be fast, small and power-efficient for that task but cannot be reprogrammed. Flexibility, like low NRE cost, is the strength of the general-purpose processor.

questions.questionText: In Vahid and Givargis's RT-level method, which sequence correctly orders the design steps of a custom single-purpose processor?
options: Write the program, convert it to an FSMD, create the datapath, then derive the controller FSM from the FSMD and the datapath
Build the controller FSM, write the program, create the datapath, then derive the FSMD
Create the datapath, write the program, convert it to an FSMD, then choose the state encoding
Convert to an FSMD, write the program, derive the controller, then create the datapath
questions.explanation: The behaviour is captured as a program and turned into an FSMD; a datapath is allocated for its variables and operations; only then is the controller FSM obtained by replacing actions with control signals and conditions with status signals.

questions.questionText: What distinguishes a finite-state machine with datapath (FSMD) from a plain FSM?
options: An FSMD has no clock and changes state asynchronously
An FSMD can have only Moore-type outputs
An FSMD adds declared variables, so its states can contain arithmetic actions on them and its transitions can test conditions on them
An FSMD always uses one-hot state encoding, while an FSM uses binary encoding
questions.explanation: An FSMD extends the FSM model with variables and data operations: states carry actions such as x = x - y and transitions carry conditions such as x < y. It is the intermediate model between a program and the datapath-plus-controller implementation.

questions.questionText: Using Vahid's templates for converting a program into an FSMD (each assignment gets its own state; a loop gets a condition state and a join state), how many states does the fragment 'while (c) { a = a + 1; }' produce?
questions.explanation: The loop becomes a condition state that tests c, one state for a = a + 1 that returns to the condition state, and a join state reached when c is false: 3 states.

questions.questionText: Using Vahid's program-to-FSMD templates (one state per assignment; a branch gets a condition state whose paths all end in a join state), how many states does 'if (c) a = b; else a = d;' produce?
questions.explanation: One condition state tests c, one state performs a = b, one performs a = d, and both paths meet in a join state: 4 states. The join state can later be removed during FSMD optimisation.

Three loops give 3 condition states and 3 join states, and the five assignments (sum = 0, i = 0, the two body statements and s_o = sum) give 5 more: 11 states. ceil(log2 11) = 4 flip-flops, because 3 bits provide only 8 codes.

questions.questionText: Why do Vahid's program-to-FSMD templates create join states such as 5-J and 6-J in the GCD FSMD?
options: They give every loop and branch one common exit point where the separate paths meet, so the templates can be chained mechanically; they perform no action and are usually removed during optimisation
They hold the arithmetic actions of the loop body
They synchronise the controller with a second clock domain
They store the return address of the loop so that it can be repeated
questions.explanation: A join state is an empty state where the paths of a branch, or the exit of a loop, come together. Because it does no work, its outgoing transition can be folded into the states before it, which is how 5-J and 6-J disappear in the optimised GCD FSMD.

questions.questionText: Why can state 1 of Vahid's unoptimised GCD FSMD, generated from the outer while (1), be eliminated during FSMD optimisation?
options: Its only transition condition is the constant 1, so it always goes to the same next state and performs no action
It performs the subtraction, which can be moved into the datapath
It is equivalent to the output state d_o = x
It is needed only for simulation, because while (1) cannot be synthesised
questions.explanation: State 1 tests a condition that is always true and has no action, so the transitions into it can go straight to its successor. The same reasoning removes the join states whose only job is to pass control on.

questions.questionText: Two consecutive FSMD states are to be merged into one state, in which both assignments complete at the same clock edge using the register values from the start of that state. Which pair of assignments CANNOT be merged without changing the result?
options: x = a + b; y = a - b
questions.explanation: In a merged state y would be computed from the old value of x, not from a + b, so y = x + 1 must stay in a later state. The other pairs have no data dependency and can share one state, as x = x_i and y = y_i do in the optimised GCD FSMD.

options: sum = 10, the same as the C program
questions.explanation: In the merged state sum adds the old i: 0 + 0, then + 1, + 2 and + 3, giving 6 when i reaches 4, instead of 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. Because sum reads the new i, the assignments are dependent and must stay in separate states, or the merged state must compute sum = sum + i + 1.

questions.questionText: A straight-line FSMD passes through 11 states once each. One state contains a multiplication with an 18 ns delay; every other state needs at most 6 ns. Design A clocks at 18 ns so that the multiply fits in one state. Design B separates the multiply into 3 states and clocks at 6 ns. What are the execution times of A and B?
questions.explanation: A: 11 states x 18 ns = 198 ns. B: the multiply now takes 3 states, so 10 + 3 = 13 states x 6 ns = 78 ns, about 2.5 times faster; 11 x 6 = 66 ns forgets the two extra states.

Registers: sum, i and s for the output. Functional units: a less-than comparator for i < n_i and two adders (sum + i and i + 1). sum and i are each written from the constant 0 and from an adder, so each needs a 2-to-1 multiplexer, while s is loaded only from sum.

questions.questionText: A datapath has four registers, each with a load enable. Three registers are fed through 2-to-1 multiplexers and the fourth through a 4-to-1 multiplexer, and an ALU performs 8 functions selected by a binary code. How many control bits must the controller supply in every state?
questions.explanation: Load enables 4 + multiplexer selects 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 5 + ALU function code ceil(log2 8) = 3, giving 4 + 5 + 3 = 12 control bits.

questions.questionText: In the GCD datapath, register x is loaded through a 2-to-1 multiplexer that selects either the input x_i or the subtractor output x - y. To carry out the FSMD action x = x - y, what must the controller do in that state?
options: Set x_sel to choose x_i and set x_ld = 1
Set x_sel to choose the subtractor output and set x_ld = 0
Set x_sel to choose the subtractor output and set x_ld = 1, keeping y_ld = 0
Set d_ld = 1 so that the result appears on d_o
questions.explanation: The multiplexer must route x - y to the input of x, and the load enable must be 1 so that x captures it at the clock edge; y_ld stays 0 so y keeps its value. This is how each FSMD action is replaced by control-signal settings in the controller.

questions.questionText: In the GCD processor the comparator output x_lt_y goes from the datapath to the controller, and x_ld goes from the controller to the datapath. What are these two signals called?
options: x_lt_y is a status signal and x_ld is a control signal
x_lt_y is a control signal and x_ld is a status signal
Both are data signals on the result bus
questions.explanation: Status signals report conditions from the datapath to the controller (x_lt_y, x_neq_y). Control signals are set by the controller to steer the datapath: register loads such as x_ld and multiplexer selects such as x_sel.

questions.questionText: In Vahid's GCD datapath the output d_o is driven by a separate register d, loaded by d_ld in the output state, rather than directly by register x. Why?
options: Because a register such as x cannot drive an output port
So that d_o holds the finished result steadily while x and y are reloaded and changed by the next computation
Because register d performs the final subtraction
So that the controller needs fewer states
questions.explanation: Register x changes throughout every computation, so connecting it to d_o would expose intermediate values. Register d captures the result once, in the output state, so d_o shows only finished results.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT an input to the combinational (next-state and output) logic of a custom processor's controller?
options: The present-state bits from the state register
Status signals from the datapath, such as x_lt_y
External control inputs, such as go_i
The full n-bit data value held in datapath register x
questions.explanation: The controller sees data only through 1-bit status signals produced by comparators in the datapath; the data words themselves stay in the datapath. Its inputs are the present state, the status signals and external control inputs.

questions.questionText: The unoptimised GCD controller has 13 states in a binary-encoded state register, 3 inputs (go_i, x_neq_y, x_lt_y) and 5 control outputs (x_sel, y_sel, x_ld, y_ld, d_ld). Its combinational logic is implemented as a ROM addressed by the state bits and the inputs, whose words hold the next state and the control outputs. What is the ROM size?
questions.explanation: State bits = ceil(log2 13) = 4, so the address has 4 + 3 = 7 bits and the ROM has 2^7 = 128 words. Each word holds 4 next-state bits + 5 outputs = 9 bits, so the ROM holds 128 x 9 = 1152 bits.

questions.questionText: A 4-state Moore controller uses binary state codes Q1Q0: S0 = 00 (wait), S1 = 01 (load x from x_i), S2 = 10 (x = x - y) and S3 = 11 (output). The load signal x_ld must be 1 in S1 and S2 only. Which expression gives x_ld?
questions.explanation: x_ld = Q1'Q0 + Q1Q0', which is Q1 XOR Q0. Q1 + Q0 would also assert x_ld in S3 (11), and Q0 alone would assert it in S3 but not in S2.

questions.questionText: The GCD processor works on 8-bit unsigned inputs x_i and y_i, and its datapath uses 8-bit unsigned registers and subtractors with no borrow or sign handling. Why can the subtraction results never be negative?
options: The controller clears a borrow flag after every subtraction
The registers are made twice the input width so that negative values fit
The subtractor saturates at zero whenever the result would be negative
Each subtraction takes the smaller value from the larger (y - x only when x < y, x - y only when x > y), so no result is ever negative
questions.explanation: The FSMD subtracts only after the comparator has shown which operand is smaller, so the result is never negative and never exceeds the larger input. That is why unsigned registers of the input width are enough.

questions.questionText: Which statement about one-hot state encoding of an N-state controller is correct?
options: It uses N flip-flops, one per state, which usually makes the next-state and output logic simpler and faster
It needs ceil(log2 N) flip-flops, the fewest possible
It leaves no unused state codes
It is another name for Gray encoding
questions.explanation: One-hot sets exactly one of N flip-flops to 1, so each output is simply the OR of the flip-flops of the states that assert it and the next-state logic is shallow. The cost is N flip-flops instead of ceil(log2 N), with 2^N - N codes unused.

questions.questionText: A controller's states are visited mostly in one fixed sequence. Which state encoding assigns codes so that consecutive states differ in only one bit, reducing flip-flop switching and hence dynamic power?
options: Output encoding, where the state codes are chosen equal to the output values
questions.explanation: In Gray encoding successive codes differ in exactly one bit, so each common transition toggles a single flip-flop. Binary counting can toggle several bits at once, for example 011 to 100.

questions.questionText: A controller with 5 states is given a 3-bit binary state register. In how many different ways can distinct 3-bit codes be assigned to the 5 states (the reason synthesis tools use heuristics instead of trying every encoding of a large FSM)?
questions.explanation: The first state can take any of 8 codes, the next any of the remaining 7, and so on: 8 x 7 x 6 x 5 x 4 = 6720 assignments. 5! = 120 counts only the orderings, and C(8, 5) = 56 ignores which state receives which code.

questions.questionText:
A Moore controller has the state table below (next state for input x = 0 and x = 1, and the output z). After state minimisation, how many states remain?

State  x=0  x=1  z
A      B    C    0
B      D    E    0
C      F    E    0
D      A    G    1
E      A    G    1
F      D    E    0
G      B    C    0
questions.explanation: Splitting by output gives {A, B, C, F, G} and {D, E}; successor groups then split the first block into {A, G} (both successors with z = 0), {B, F} (both with z = 1) and {C} (one of each). A further pass changes nothing, so {A, G}, {B, F}, {C} and {D, E} remain: 4 states.

questions.questionText: An FSMD has three states. S1 computes t1 = a + b and t2 = c + d, S2 computes t3 = t1 + t2, and S3 computes t4 = t3 + a, t5 = t3 + b and t6 = t3 + c. Additions in the same state need separate adders, but adders may be shared between states. What is the minimum number of adders, compared with one-to-one allocation?
options: 6 instead of 6, because no sharing is possible
questions.explanation: The minimum equals the largest number of additions in any one state: max(2, 1, 3) = 3. One-to-one allocation uses one adder per operation, 6, so sharing saves 3 adders at the cost of multiplexers on the adder inputs.

questions.questionText: An FSMD passes through states S1 to S8 in order. Each variable is live from the state that writes it to the last state that reads it, inclusive: a S1-S3, b S2-S4, f S3-S5, c S4-S6, d S5-S8, e S7-S8. Two variables may share a register only if their live ranges have no state in common. What is the minimum number of registers?
questions.explanation: At most 3 variables are live in the same state (a, b, f in S3; b, f, c in S4; f, c, d in S5), so 3 registers are needed, and 3 suffice: R1 = a, c, e; R2 = b, d; R3 = f. One-to-one allocation would use 6.

questions.questionText: Which pair of operations in an FSMD can be bound to a single shared subtractor?
options: a - b and c - d, both in state S3
y - x in state S6 and x - y in state S7
x - y and x + y, both in state S4
Any two subtractions, whatever states they are in
questions.explanation: A functional unit can be shared only by operations that are never needed in the same clock cycle, i.e. operations in different states; the GCD subtractions y - x and x - y qualify. Two subtractions in the same state need two subtractors.

questions.questionText: A datapath uses an adder in state S2 and a subtractor in state S5. The designer replaces both with one ALU that can add or subtract. Which statement is correct?
options: The ALU needs no extra control, because it detects from its inputs which operation is needed
The controller must also drive the ALU's function-select input, and input multiplexers are needed if the two operations read different registers
The change is impossible, because an ALU can be used in only one state
The ALU replaces the controller, so the FSM is no longer needed
questions.explanation: A multi-function unit can be shared by operations in different states, but the controller must set its function code in each state. Multiplexers are needed on the ALU inputs when the two operations take their operands from different registers.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit subtractor costs 40 gate equivalents and an 8-bit 2-to-1 multiplexer costs 24. The GCD datapath's two subtractors (x - y and y - x) are replaced by one shared subtractor with a 2-to-1 multiplexer on each of its two inputs. What is the effect on datapath area?
questions.explanation: Unshared: 2 x 40 = 80 gate equivalents. Shared: 40 + 2 x 24 = 88, so sharing adds 8 gate equivalents here and also lengthens the critical path; it pays off only when the shared unit is much larger than the multiplexers it needs.

questions.questionText: In the GCD datapath the longest path runs from register x (clock-to-Q 1 ns) through a subtractor (6 ns) and the 2-to-1 register-input multiplexer (1 ns) to the setup of register x (0.5 ns). Sharing one subtractor for x - y and y - x adds a 1 ns 2-to-1 multiplexer in front of each subtractor input. For a computation that takes 15 clock cycles, what are the execution times without and with sharing?
questions.explanation: Unshared: T = 1 + 6 + 1 + 0.5 = 8.5 ns, so 15 x 8.5 = 127.5 ns. Shared: the two input multiplexers work in parallel and add one 1 ns delay, so T = 9.5 ns and 15 x 9.5 = 142.5 ns.

questions.questionText: A custom processor has three register-to-register paths: register x to subtractor to multiplexer to register x (1 + 6 + 1 + 0.5 ns); register x to comparator to controller next-state logic to state register (1 + 4 + 2 + 0.5 ns); state register to output logic to multiplexer select to register x (1 + 1.5 + 1 + 0.5 ns). What is the maximum clock frequency?
questions.explanation: The clock period must cover the slowest path: max(8.5, 7.5, 4.0) = 8.5 ns, so f_max = 1 / 8.5 ns = 117.6 MHz. Adding the paths (20 ns, 50 MHz) is wrong because they all operate in parallel within the same cycle.

questions.questionText: According to Vahid and Givargis, when optimising a custom single-purpose processor, at which level are the largest improvements usually obtained?
questions.explanation: A better algorithm changes the number of operations and iterations fundamentally, as in GCD, where the modulo version needs about log(max) iterations instead of up to max(x, y). FSMD, datapath and FSM optimisations then refine that result.

questions.questionText: GCD(100, 3) is computed two ways. Version 1 repeats 'if (x < y) y = y - x; else x = x - y;' while x != y. Version 2 (Euclid) repeats 'r = x mod y; x = y; y = r;' while y != 0. How many loop iterations does each version perform?
questions.explanation: Version 1 subtracts 3 from x 33 times (100 down to 1), then (1, 3) to (1, 2) to (1, 1): 35 iterations. Version 2 goes (100, 3) to (3, 1) to (1, 0): 2 iterations, trading a much larger divider for far fewer iterations.

questions.questionText: In the optimised GCD FSMD, state 5 chooses among three successors: y = y - x (when x < y), x = x - y (when x > y) and d_o = x (when x = y). What is the minimum number of 1-bit status signals the datapath must send to the controller for this decision?
questions.explanation: Three outcomes need at least ceil(log2 3) = 2 bits, for example x_lt_y and x_neq_y, since x > y is x_neq_y AND NOT x_lt_y. A single bit can distinguish only two outcomes.

questions.questionText: For operands needing s subtractions, the unoptimised 13-state GCD FSMD takes 4s + 5 clock cycles from loading the operands to writing d_o, while the optimised 6-state FSMD takes 2s + 3. How many clock cycles does the optimisation save for x_i = 45 and y_i = 12?
questions.explanation: The pairs run (45, 12), (33, 12), (21, 12), (9, 12), (9, 3), (6, 3), (3, 3), so s = 6. Unoptimised 4 x 6 + 5 = 29 cycles and optimised 2 x 6 + 3 = 15 cycles, a saving of 14 cycles.

questions.questionText: A GPP at 100 MHz runs the GCD loop with 6 instructions per iteration at an average CPI of 1.5. A custom GCD processor at 50 MHz takes 2 clock cycles per iteration. For 1000 iterations, how do they compare?
options: The custom processor is 4.5 times faster
The custom processor is 2.25 times faster
The custom processor is 1.5 times faster
questions.explanation: GPP: 1000 x 6 x 1.5 = 9000 cycles x 10 ns = 90 µs. Custom: 1000 x 2 = 2000 cycles x 20 ns = 40 µs, so the custom processor is 90 / 40 = 2.25 times faster; the cycle ratio 9 / 2 = 4.5 ignores its slower clock.

Signal assignments take effect together when the process suspends, so both right-hand sides use the old values: edge 1 gives x = 9 and y = 5 + 1 = 6, edge 2 gives x = 6 and y = 9 + 1 = 10. Reading the assignments one after another as in C would give x = 10, y = 11.
The operands go (20, 8), (12, 8), (4, 8), (4, 4), so s = 3 subtractions. Edges: S_LOAD 1 + S_CMP 4 + subtraction states 3 + S_OUT 1 = 9 (that is 2s + 3), and d_o = 4.

subtopics.title: General-Purpose Processors: Architecture, Operation & Programmer's View
subtopics.subtitle: Datapath and control unit, fetch-decode-execute, instruction set, addressing modes, dev tools

concepts.text: Basic Architecture

A general-purpose processor is a programmable digital system built for a wide variety of applications rather than one task: the manufacturer sells the same chip to many customers, spreading its NRE cost, and each customer supplies a program. For the embedded designer this gives low NRE, high flexibility, short time-to-market and low unit cost at small volumes, at the price of higher power and lower performance than a custom design because the general datapath carries hardware the program may never use. Internally every general-purpose processor consists of a datapath, a control unit and memory connected by buses.
Datapath: the part that manipulates data:
items: Arithmetic logic unit (ALU) performing add, subtract, AND, OR, shift and compare, and producing status flags (zero, carry, overflow, sign).
Registers: a small number of fast storage locations (general-purpose registers and the accumulator) holding operands and results.
Internal buses that move data between registers, the ALU and the memory interface; the bit width N (8, 16, 32 or 64) of the datapath usually fixes the word size of registers, buses and ALU.

concepts.text: Control unit and memory:
items: Program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction; instruction register (IR) holds the instruction just fetched.
Controller: an FSM (hardwired) or a microprogram that decodes the IR and sequences the datapath, memory and PC through each instruction.

Memory holds both the program (instructions) and the data. Princeton (von Neumann) architecture uses one memory and one bus for both; Harvard architecture uses separate instruction and data memories so a fetch and a data access can overlap, common in microcontrollers and DSPs.

Cache: small fast SRAM near the processor that keeps recently used instructions and data; most processors have separate instruction and data caches, forming a hierarchy of registers, cache, main memory and secondary storage.

concepts.text: Operation
Instruction execution: the processor repeats the instruction cycle for each instruction:
items: Fetch: read the instruction at the PC address into the IR and increment the PC.
Decode: the controller determines the operation and the operands required.
Fetch operands: read operands from registers or memory into the ALU inputs.
Execute: the ALU or other datapath unit performs the operation.
Store results: write the result back to a register or memory; branch instructions instead update the PC.
