concepts.text: Pipelining overlaps these stages like an assembly line: while one instruction executes, the next is decoded and a third is fetched, so a k-stage pipeline can approach k times the throughput of a non-pipelined processor once full, though branches and data dependencies (hazards) cause stalls. Superscalar processors go further by fetching and issuing several instructions per cycle to multiple ALUs with dynamic hardware scheduling. VLIW (very long instruction word) processors also execute several operations per cycle, but the compiler packs them statically into one wide instruction, which keeps the hardware simple and is popular in DSPs.

concepts.plainText: Pipeline speedup S = n k / (k + n - 1) for n instructions on k stages

concepts.text: Programmer's View
What the programmer sees (the instruction-set architecture):
items: Instruction set grouped as data transfer (MOV, LOAD, STORE, PUSH, POP), arithmetic and logic (ADD, SUB, MUL, AND, OR, XOR, shift, compare) and control flow (JMP, conditional branch, CALL, RET, interrupt return).
Program memory space and data memory space: with an n-bit address the processor can reach 2^n locations; program code, constants, stack and heap are laid out inside these spaces.
Registers visible to software: general-purpose registers, the PC, stack pointer (SP) and status or flag register; special-function registers configure peripherals in microcontrollers.
Programs may be written in assembly language, one mnemonic per machine instruction, or in a structured language such as C that a compiler translates into many instructions.

rows: Inside the instruction itself as a constant
In the register named by the instruction
In memory at the address held in a register
In memory at the address given in the instruction
The instruction gives a memory address that holds the operand's address

concepts.text: I/O from the programmer's side is either memory-mapped, where peripheral registers occupy addresses in the normal memory space and ordinary load and store instructions access them, or standard (port-mapped), where special IN and OUT instructions address a separate I/O space. Interrupts let a peripheral suspend the current program: the processor finishes the current instruction, saves the PC, jumps to the interrupt service routine at the address given in the vector table, and returns with an interrupt-return instruction; the programmer writes the ISR and enables the interrupt through control registers. An operating system, when present, adds process scheduling, memory management, device drivers and system calls; many small embedded systems run without one and use a simple polling loop or a lightweight RTOS.
Development Environment

Embedded software is written and compiled on a development processor (the host PC) but executed on the target processor, so the tools are cross-tools. The design flow is: write assembly or C source files; the assembler or compiler translates each into an object file; the linker combines object files and libraries into a single executable image with resolved addresses; the image is tested on an instruction-set simulator, a development board or through an in-circuit emulator under a debugger; finally the image is programmed into the target's Flash or ROM. Integrated development environments bundle all of these with an editor and project manager.

rows: Translates assembly mnemonics into machine code object files, resolving labels and symbols
Translates a high-level language such as C into assembly or machine code, with optimisation for size or speed
Combines object files and libraries, assigns final addresses and produces the executable image (HEX/ELF)
Lets the programmer set breakpoints, single-step, and inspect registers and memory of a running program
Software on the host that models the target processor cycle by cycle so code can run before hardware exists
Hardware that replaces or attaches to the target processor and gives real-time, full-speed debugging in the real system
Ready-made board with the target processor, memory and I/O for early hardware testing and prototyping

concepts.text: Application-specific versus general-purpose, and how to select a processor:
items: Application-specific processors (ASIPs, custom hardware) win on performance, power and unit cost at high volume; general-purpose processors win on NRE, flexibility, tool availability and time-to-market.

Selection metrics: clock frequency and MIPS or benchmark scores (Dhrystone, EEMBC), datapath width, on-chip memory and peripherals, power and voltage range, package size, unit cost and volume pricing, quality of compilers, debuggers and vendor support.
A raw MIPS number is not comparable across architectures because instructions do different amounts of work; use benchmarks that resemble the actual application.
Match the processor to the task: a general-purpose 32-bit core for control-heavy software, a DSP for signal processing, a microcontroller for cheap I/O-centric control.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Inside a General-Purpose Processor

Vahid and Givargis build a general-purpose processor as if it were a single-purpose processor whose one job is to execute instructions. Its controller is an FSMD with a Fetch state (IR ← M[PC], PC ← PC + 1), a Decode state that branches on the opcode, and one or more execute states for each instruction, all returning to Fetch; the control unit holds the PC and IR, while the datapath holds a register file and an ALU connected to memory. Because each state lasts one clock cycle, an instruction takes as many cycles as the states it visits, and the clock period must cover the slowest register-to-register path in any state, which is usually the memory access.

rows: If Rn = 0 then PC ← PC + rel

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: total = 10 + 9 + ... + 1 on the simple instruction set
0       MOV R0, #0     ; total = 0
1       MOV R1, #10    ; i = 10
2       MOV R2, #1     ; constant 1
3       MOV R3, #0     ; constant 0
4 Loop: JZ  R1, Next   ; leave when i = 0
5       ADD R0, R1     ; total += i
6       SUB R1, R2     ; i--
7       JZ  R3, Loop   ; always jumps, since R3 = 0
Executed: 4 MOV + 11 x JZ R1 + 10 x (ADD, SUB, JZ R3) = 45 instructions
At 3 cycles each (Fetch, Decode, one execute state) = 135 cycles
At 50 MHz: 135 x 20 ns = 2.7 µs, and R0 = 55

An issue width w sets the best-case CPI at 1/w, but real code rarely reaches it: an instruction cannot issue in the same cycle as one it depends on, so superscalar hardware checks register dependences every cycle, and an in-order core issues only the older instruction of a dependent pair. A VLIW processor moves that work to the compiler, which fills each long word with independent operations and pads the empty slots with NOPs; the hardware is simpler and uses less power, but the code grows and binaries are tied to one machine's slot count and latencies. Branches hurt every pipeline: without prediction, a taken branch resolved at the end of stage s discards the s − 1 instructions fetched behind it.

concepts.plainText: Cycles for N independent instructions on a w-issue, k-stage pipeline = (k − 1) + ceil(N / w); w = 1 gives the scalar pipeline

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: 40 independent instructions, 5 stages (k = 5)
Non-pipelined, 1 cycle per stage : 40 x 5          = 200 cycles
Scalar pipeline                  : (5 - 1) + 40    = 44 cycles
2-issue superscalar              : (5 - 1) + 40/2  = 24 cycles
One taken branch resolved in stage 4 (scalar): 44 + 3 = 47 cycles
VLIW, 4 slots x 32 bits, 14 operations packed into 5 words:
  slots = 20, NOPs = 20 - 14 = 6 (30 %)
  code  = 5 x 16 bytes = 80 bytes, against 14 x 4 = 56 bytes on a scalar RISC

To the programmer memory is an array of bytes, but three details decide whether code is correct and fast. Byte order: a little-endian processor (x86, most ARM systems) stores the least significant byte of a word at the lowest address and a big-endian one the most significant byte, which matters whenever words are read through byte pointers or sent over a link. Alignment: compilers pad structures so that each field sits at a multiple of its own size, so a peripheral register's offset in a struct overlay is counted in bytes, including padding. Locality: the cache is invisible to the instruction set, yet a loop that walks a row-major array column by column can need a new cache block on every access, while the row-by-row loop misses only once per block.

A typical assembler makes two passes: pass 1 steps a location counter through the source, adding each instruction's size and entering every label's address in a symbol table, and pass 2 emits the machine code, now able to fill in forward references. Object files are relocatable, so the linker places each section at its final address (rounding up for alignment), adds that base to every relocatable reference and writes an image such as ELF or Intel HEX, whose records end in a checksum that the device programmer verifies. An ISS gives full controllability and observability but runs slowly and without the real environment, whereas an in-circuit emulator or on-chip debug logic reached over JTAG or SWD runs the real chip at full speed; software breakpoints patch a break instruction into writable memory, so code in ROM needs hardware breakpoint comparators.

Worked example 3: choosing a processor (all candidates share one ISA)
Workload: 0.9 M instructions every 10 ms, processor load at most 75 %
Required rate = 0.9 M / 10 ms = 90 MIPS; 90 / 0.75 = 120 MIPS
X: 300 MHz, CPI 2.0 -> 150 MIPS  meets, $4.20
Y: 200 MHz, CPI 1.5 -> 133 MIPS  meets, $3.10
Z: 250 MHz, CPI 2.5 -> 100 MIPS  fails despite its clock
Choose Y, the cheapest candidate that meets the requirement
Across different ISAs use benchmarks instead of native MIPS:
DMIPS = Dhrystones per second / 1757, e.g. 1,405,600 / 1757 = 800 DMIPS

Common slips: a loop that runs n times executes its exit test n + 1 times; the k − 1 fill cycles are added once, not divided by the issue width; NOP slots of a VLIW word still occupy program memory; a memory-mapped register's address is base plus its byte offset including padding, not base plus its field number; an n-bit program counter that addresses instruction words reaches 2^n words, i.e. 2^n times the word size in bytes; and native MIPS figures compare fairly only between processors with the same instruction set.

formulas.plainText: CPU time = instruction count x cycles per instruction / clock frequency
MIPS = f_clk / (CPI x 10^6)

formulas.latex: S = \frac{n k}{k + n - 1} \rightarrow k \text{ as } n \to \infty
formulas.plainText: k-stage pipeline speedup S = nk / (k + n - 1), approaching k
n address bits reach 2^n locations

notes.text: For addressing-mode questions ask where the operand lives: in the instruction (immediate), in a register (register-direct), in memory via a register (register-indirect), in memory via an address in the instruction (direct) or via an address stored at that address (indirect).

An instruction-set simulator runs on the host and models the target in software; an in-circuit emulator is hardware plugged into the real target system. Do not swap the two when asked which one runs at full speed on real I/O.

Harvard architecture is standard in microcontrollers such as the 8051 and AVR and in DSPs; Princeton (von Neumann) is standard in PCs and in the 8085 and 8086. Many modern processors are Princeton at the main memory but Harvard at the cache level (separate instruction and data caches).

formulas.title: CPU execution time
formulas.plainText: t_CPU = IC x CPI / f_clk
formulas.description: Time to run a program of IC instructions with average CPI cycles per instruction at clock frequency f_clk; a program of 10^6 instructions at CPI 2 on 100 MHz takes 20 ms.

formulas.title: MIPS rating
formulas.plainText: MIPS = f_clk / (CPI x 10^6)
formulas.description: Millions of instructions per second; a simple processor-selection metric that is only meaningful between processors with similar instruction sets.

formulas.title: Pipeline speedup
formulas.plainText: S = n k / (k + n - 1)
formulas.description: Ideal speedup of a k-stage pipeline over a non-pipelined processor for n instructions; 100 instructions on 5 stages give 500 / 104 = 4.81, approaching 5 for large n.

formulas.title: Memory address space
formulas.plainText: N = 2^n locations for n address bits
formulas.description: Size of the program or data memory space visible to the programmer; 16 address bits give 64 K locations, 32 bits give 4 G.

flashcards.front: What are the five stages of instruction execution in a general-purpose processor?
flashcards.back: Fetch the instruction (PC to IR), decode it, fetch operands, execute in the ALU, and store the result; branches update the PC instead of storing a result.

flashcards.front: Distinguish Princeton (von Neumann) and Harvard memory architectures.
flashcards.back: Princeton shares one memory and bus for instructions and data; Harvard has separate instruction and data memories and buses so a fetch and a data access can happen in the same cycle.

flashcards.front: What do the assembler, linker and instruction-set simulator each do in the embedded development flow?
flashcards.back: The assembler converts mnemonics to object code, the linker merges object files and libraries into one image with final addresses, and the ISS runs that image on the host by modelling the target processor so testing can begin before hardware exists.

flashcards.front: How does superscalar differ from VLIW?
flashcards.back: Both execute several instructions per cycle: superscalar hardware finds independent instructions dynamically at run time, while VLIW relies on the compiler to pack independent operations into one long instruction word statically.

questions.questionText: A program of 1,000,000 instructions runs on a general-purpose processor with an average CPI of 2 at a clock frequency of 100 MHz. Its execution time is:
Which development tool runs on the host computer and models the target processor in software so that embedded code can be tested before the target hardware is available?
questions.explanation: An instruction-set simulator (ISS) executes the target's machine code on the development processor; an in-circuit emulator and a development board require real hardware.

questions.questionText: In which addressing mode does the instruction contain a memory address, and the memory location at that address holds the address of the actual operand?
questions.explanation: Indirect addressing needs two memory accesses: one to read the operand's address from the location named in the instruction, and one to read the operand. Direct addressing reads the operand from the named location itself.

questions.questionText: A 5-stage pipelined processor executes a sequence of 100 instructions. Ignoring hazards, its speedup over an equivalent non-pipelined processor is approximately:
questions.explanation: S = nk / (k + n - 1) = 100 x 5 / (5 + 100 - 1) = 500 / 104 = 4.81. The ideal value of 5 is reached only as n becomes very large.

questions.questionText: In Vahid and Givargis's model of a general-purpose processor, which of these components belongs to the control unit rather than to the datapath?
options: The multiplexers that route operands to the ALU
questions.explanation: The control unit contains the controller, the program counter and the instruction register; the ALU, the registers and their routing multiplexers form the datapath that the controller drives.

questions.questionText: A microcontroller is described as an 8-bit processor. What does '8-bit' normally refer to?
options: The width of its datapath: its ALU, data registers and internal data bus handle 8 bits at a time
The width of its address bus, so it can address only 256 bytes
The number of general-purpose registers it contains
The length of every one of its instructions
questions.explanation: An N-bit processor has an N-bit datapath (ALU, registers and buses). The address bus is usually wider (the 8-bit 8051 and 8085 use 16-bit addresses), and instructions may be one to several bytes long.

questions.questionText: In a general-purpose processor, what does the size (number of bits) of the program counter determine?
options: The width of the ALU and the data registers
The number of instructions that can be in the pipeline at once
The maximum clock frequency of the processor
How large an address space instructions can be fetched from
questions.explanation: The PC holds instruction addresses, so an n-bit PC can reach 2^n instruction locations; the datapath width and the clock frequency are set by other parts of the design.

questions.questionText: According to Vahid and Givargis, the clock period of a general-purpose processor must be at least as long as:
options: The sum of the delays of all the stages an instruction passes through
The longest register-to-register delay anywhere in the processor, which is often a memory access
The average of all the register-to-register delays in the processor
The shortest register-to-register delay, so that fast operations are not slowed down
questions.explanation: Every register must capture a settled value at each clock edge, so the slowest register-to-register path (commonly a memory read) sets the minimum clock period and hence the maximum clock frequency.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the datapath and the control unit of a general-purpose processor is NOT correct?
options: The controller sets the datapath's control inputs, such as multiplexer selects, register load enables and the ALU function
The datapath holds the program counter and decodes the opcode of each instruction
The datapath sends status signals, such as the ALU's zero flag, back to the controller for conditional branches
A load copies a word from memory into a datapath register, and a store copies a register into memory
questions.explanation: The program counter, the instruction register and opcode decoding belong to the control unit; the datapath only stores and transforms data under the controller's direction.

questions.questionText: A simple processor has 16-bit instructions: bits 15–12 are the opcode, bits 11–8 name register Rn, and bits 7–0 hold a direct address or an immediate constant. Opcode 0001 is MOV direct, Rn (M[direct] ← Rn) and opcode 0011 is MOV Rn, #imm (Rn ← imm). What happens when the two instruction words 3105H and then 1120H are executed?
options: R1 is loaded with the contents of address 05H, and then that value is stored at address 20H
R1 is loaded with 5, and then R1 is loaded with the contents of address 20H
R5 is loaded with 1, and then 1 is stored at address 20H
R1 is loaded with 5, and then 5 is stored at memory address 20H

questions.questionText:
A processor provides MOV Rn, #imm (Rn ← imm), MOV Rn, direct (Rn ← M[direct]), MOV direct, Rn (M[direct] ← Rn), MOV @Rn, Rm (M[Rn] ← Rm) and ADD Rn, Rm (Rn ← Rn + Rm). The program below runs with M[5] = 9 and every other memory word 0 (all addresses and values decimal). What are M[20] and M[21] afterwards?

MOV R0, #20
MOV R1, 5
MOV R2, #3
ADD R1, R2
MOV @R0, R1
MOV 21, R0
questions.explanation: R0 = 20, R1 = M[5] = 9, R2 = 3, then R1 = 9 + 3 = 12; MOV @R0, R1 stores 12 at the address held in R0 (20), and MOV 21, R0 stores R0 = 20 at address 21. Reading MOV R1, 5 as an immediate would give 8.

questions.questionText:
The program below uses MOV Rn, #imm (Rn ← imm), ADD Rn, Rm (Rn ← Rn + Rm), SUB Rn, Rm (Rn ← Rn − Rm) and JZ Rn, label (jump to label when Rn = 0). Counting from the first MOV and not counting the instruction at Next, how many instructions are executed, and what does R0 hold on reaching Next?

      MOV R0, #0
      MOV R1, #6
      MOV R2, #1
      MOV R3, #0
Loop: JZ  R1, Next
      ADD R0, R1
      SUB R1, R2
      JZ  R3, Loop
Next: ...
questions.explanation: 4 MOVs + the loop test JZ R1 executed 7 times (6 passes plus the exit) + 6 × (ADD, SUB, JZ R3) = 4 + 7 + 18 = 29 instructions, and R0 = 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 21.

questions.questionText:
The program below (MOV Rn, #imm loads a constant, ADD/SUB Rn, Rm put Rn + Rm or Rn − Rm into Rn, and JZ Rn, label jumps when Rn = 0) runs on a non-pipelined processor. Every instruction needs 1 fetch cycle and 1 decode cycle; after that, MOV Rn, #imm and JZ need 1 execute cycle, while ADD and SUB need 2. With a 25 MHz clock, how many clock cycles and how much time does the program take up to reaching Next?

      MOV R0, #0
      MOV R1, #10
      MOV R2, #1
      MOV R3, #0
Loop: JZ  R1, Next
      ADD R0, R1
      SUB R1, R2
      JZ  R3, Loop
Next: ...
questions.explanation: 45 instructions execute: 4 MOV and 21 JZ (11 + 10) at 3 cycles = 75 cycles, plus 10 ADD and 10 SUB at 4 cycles = 80 cycles, total 155 × 40 ns = 6.2 µs. Charging every instruction 3 cycles gives 135, and forgetting the final JZ gives 152.

questions.questionText: In which step of the instruction cycle does the processor copy the instruction addressed by the PC into the instruction register and advance the PC to the next sequential instruction?
questions.explanation: Fetch performs IR ← M[PC] and PC ← PC + 1; decode then works out the operation, and only a branch later overwrites the PC.

questions.questionText: Instructions pass through five stages (fetch, decode, fetch operands, execute, store results), one clock cycle each, in a pipeline that keeps fetching sequentially. The 3rd instruction is a taken branch whose outcome is known at the end of its execute stage; the instructions fetched after it are then discarded, and fetching restarts at the target in the next cycle. If 8 instructions complete in total (3 up to and including the branch, then 5 from the target) and there are no other stalls, how many clock cycles does the sequence take?
questions.explanation: The branch is fetched in cycle 3 and resolved at the end of cycle 6, so the target is fetched in cycle 7 and the 5th target instruction, fetched in cycle 11, finishes in cycle 15. The 3 discarded fetches add 3 cycles to the ideal 5 + 8 − 1 = 12; without pipelining 8 × 5 = 40 cycles would be needed.

questions.questionText: A 2-issue superscalar processor has 5-stage pipelines and runs 100 mutually independent instructions, issuing two in every cycle with no stalls. How many clock cycles pass from the first fetch until the last instruction completes?
questions.explanation: Cycles = (k − 1) + N / w = 4 + 100 / 2 = 54. A single-issue pipeline needs 4 + 100 = 104, and 50 forgets the 4 fill cycles.

questions.questionText: A VLIW processor fetches 128-bit instruction words, each holding four 32-bit operation slots. Because of data dependences, the compiler schedules a loop body of 18 operations into 7 instruction words and fills the unused slots with NOPs. What fraction of the slots are NOPs, and how many bytes of program memory does the loop body occupy?
questions.explanation: 7 words × 4 slots = 28 slots, of which 28 − 18 = 10 are NOPs (10 / 28 = 35.7 %); the code takes 7 × 128 bits = 7 × 16 = 112 bytes, against 18 × 4 = 72 bytes for a scalar RISC with 32-bit instructions.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a recognised disadvantage of VLIW processors compared with superscalar processors?
options: They need complex hardware to detect dependences and schedule instructions at run time
They can never complete more than one operation per clock cycle
They cannot run programs written in a high-level language
Code is usually larger because unused slots hold NOPs, and programs generally must be recompiled when the number or latency of the functional units changes
questions.explanation: VLIW scheduling is static: the compiler fixes which operations share a word, so the hardware stays simple, but NOP padding enlarges the code and the schedule is tied to one implementation. Run-time dependence checking is the cost paid by superscalar designs.

questions.questionText: Which statement about a superscalar processor is correct?
options: Its hardware checks dependences at run time and issues several independent instructions per clock to parallel units, so the average CPI can fall below 1
Its compiler must pack parallel operations into one long instruction word before they can execute together
Programs must be rewritten in a special parallel instruction set before more than one ALU can be used
Its best possible CPI is 1, as in any pipelined processor
questions.explanation: A superscalar core finds instruction-level parallelism dynamically and runs ordinary binaries of its ISA; packing by the compiler describes VLIW, and issuing w instructions per cycle allows a CPI as low as 1/w.

questions.questionText:
A 2-issue in-order superscalar processor issues at most two instructions per cycle, strictly in program order (ADD R1, R2, R3 means R1 ← R2 + R3). A result can be used only by instructions issued in a later cycle than its producer, and if the older instruction of a candidate pair can issue but the younger cannot, only the older one issues. How many issue cycles does this sequence need?

I1: ADD R1, R2, R3
I2: SUB R4, R1, R5
I3: AND R6, R7, R8
I4: OR  R9, R6, R2
I5: XOR R10, R11, R12
I6: ADD R13, R10, R4
questions.explanation: Cycle 1: I1 alone (I2 needs R1); cycle 2: I2 and I3; cycle 3: I4 and I5; cycle 4: I6, which needs R10 from I5. Ignoring the dependences would give 3 cycles, and single issue 6.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the Princeton (von Neumann) memory architecture is correct?
options: Instructions and data are kept in separate memories with separate address spaces and buses
Instructions and data share one memory and one bus, so an instruction fetch and a data access cannot take place in the same memory cycle
It is chosen mainly in DSPs so that an instruction and two operands can be fetched in one cycle
It prevents a program from reading constant tables stored alongside its code
questions.explanation: Princeton uses a single memory space for program and data, which is simple and flexible but makes fetches and data accesses take turns; separate memories and buses define the Harvard architecture used in many DSPs and microcontrollers.
A little-endian processor stores the least significant byte at the lowest address, so the bytes of x in memory are 78, 56, 34, 12; p[0] = 78 and p[3] = 12. A big-endian processor would print 12 78.

questions.questionText: The array int a[128][128] (4-byte int, stored row-major, starting on a cache-block boundary) is summed once by loop A, for (i…) for (j…) sum += a[i][j];, and once by loop B, which swaps the loops so that j is outer and i inner. The data cache is 8 KB (1 KB = 1024 bytes), direct-mapped, with 32-byte blocks; it is empty at the start of each loop, and only the array accesses use it. What are the miss rates of loops A and B?
questions.explanation: Loop A reads consecutive ints, so each 32-byte block gives 1 miss and 7 hits (1/8 = 12.5 %). Loop B strides 128 × 4 = 512 bytes, so every access needs a different block, and the 128 blocks of a column map onto only 16 of the 256 lines, evicting one another before the next column reuses them: every access misses.

questions.questionText: From the programmer's point of view, which statement about a processor's data cache is correct?
options: The program must execute a special instruction to copy each variable into the cache before using it
The cache has its own addresses, and each load chooses whether to address the cache or main memory
Ordinary loads and stores use the cache automatically, code with good locality runs faster, and memory-mapped peripheral registers are normally placed in a non-cacheable region
Reading a cached status register of a peripheral always returns the device's latest status
questions.explanation: A cache is transparent to the instruction set: it keeps copies of recently used main-memory blocks without being addressed directly. A cached device register could return a stale copy, so I/O regions are marked non-cacheable.

questions.questionText: A Harvard-architecture microcontroller has a 16-bit program counter that addresses program memory in 16-bit instruction words, and its data memory uses 16-bit byte addresses. What are the largest program memory, in bytes, and the largest data memory it can address (1 KB = 1024 bytes)?
options: 64 KB of program memory and 64 KB of data memory
128 KB of program memory and 64 KB of data memory
64 KB in total, shared by program and data
128 KB of program memory and 128 KB of data memory
questions.explanation: The PC reaches 2^16 = 65,536 words of 2 bytes = 128 KB of program memory, while the separate data space has 2^16 byte addresses = 64 KB. Taking the PC as a byte address gives 64 KB, and a shared space is the Princeton view.

questions.questionText: A compiler for a processor offering immediate, register-direct, register-indirect, direct and memory-indirect addressing translates the C constructs below. Which pairing of C construct and addressing mode is correct?
options: x = 5; with the constant 5 placed in the instruction — direct addressing
y = *p; with the pointer p held in register R2 — immediate addressing
z = a + b; with a, b and z all held in registers — memory-indirect addressing
Reading a global variable whose fixed address is known at link time — direct addressing
questions.explanation: A constant inside the instruction is immediate, *p through a register is register-indirect, and operands already in registers use register-direct addressing; a variable at a fixed address named in the instruction uses direct addressing.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit processor provides ADD (add two bytes) and ADC (add two bytes plus the carry flag). What is the minimum number of add instructions needed to add two 32-bit unsigned integers stored as bytes in memory?
questions.explanation: 32 / 8 = 4 byte additions: ADD for the least significant byte, then three ADCs that each add in the carry from the byte below.

Offsets are in bytes: CR 0x0, SR 0x4, DR 0x8 (2 bytes), RSV 0xA (2 bytes), BRR 0xC, so the write goes to 0x40011000 + 0xC = 0x4001100C. Counting fields gives 0x40011003, and leaving out RSV gives 0x4001100A.

questions.questionText: In the 8086 the interrupt vector table occupies the lowest 1 KB of memory, and each interrupt type n has a 4-byte entry (offset word, then segment word). At which physical addresses is the vector for type 21H stored?
questions.explanation: The entry for type n starts at 4 × n = 4 × 21H = 84H, so bytes 00084H–00087H hold the ISR's offset (IP) and segment (CS).

questions.questionText: Why does an interrupt service routine end with a return-from-interrupt instruction (IRET on the 8086, RETI on the 8051) rather than an ordinary subroutine return?
options: It also restores state that interrupt entry saved or changed besides the return address, such as the flags on the 8086 or the interrupt-in-progress priority logic on the 8051
An ordinary return instruction cannot pop an address from the stack
It is shorter, so it saves program memory in every ISR
It automatically clears the peripheral's interrupt request flag, so the ISR never needs to do so
questions.explanation: Interrupt entry saves more than the PC (the 8086 pushes the flags) or changes processor state (the 8051 marks a priority level as in service), and only the return-from-interrupt instruction undoes it; RET would leave the flags or the priority logic wrong.

questions.questionText: On a typical microcontroller, a timer overflow sets the timer's maskable interrupt flag. Which conditions must all hold for this event to run the timer's interrupt service routine?
options: Interrupts are enabled globally, because the global enable automatically enables every source
The timer's own source is enabled; the global enable affects only non-maskable interrupts
None, because a flag set by hardware always forces a jump to the ISR
An ISR is provided at the timer's vector, that interrupt source is enabled (unmasked), and interrupts are enabled globally
questions.explanation: A maskable interrupt passes two gates: the source's own enable or mask bit (ET0 on the 8051, its NVIC enable bit on a Cortex-M) and the global enable (EA on the 8051, PRIMASK clear on a Cortex-M); the vector then supplies the ISR address. With either gate closed the flag simply stays set until polled or enabled.

questions.questionText: Which of these jobs is done by an operating system rather than by a development tool?
options: Resolving references between object files and fixing their final addresses
Translating assembly mnemonics into machine code
Sharing processor time among several tasks and managing memory and devices for them at run time
Writing the executable image into the target's flash memory
questions.explanation: Scheduling and resource management happen at run time and belong to the OS; the other jobs are done before the program runs, by the linker, the assembler and the device programmer.

questions.questionText: Many small microcontroller-based products run their program directly on the hardware, with no operating system. What is the usual reason?
options: A processor without an operating system cannot respond to interrupts
The product performs one fixed job that a main loop plus interrupt service routines can handle, so an OS would only add memory, CPU-time and complexity costs
C compilers can only generate code for processors that run an operating system
An operating system can only run on a processor with a Harvard architecture
questions.explanation: An OS pays off when many tasks must share the processor or rich services such as files and networking are needed; a single-function device with a few kilobytes of RAM is usually simpler and more predictable as a super-loop with ISRs.

questions.questionText: A compiler runs on a PC (the development processor) but produces machine code for an ARM microcontroller (the target processor). What is it called?
questions.explanation: A cross-compiler generates code for a processor other than the one it runs on; embedded tool chains (cross-assembler, cross-compiler and linker) all work this way.

questions.questionText:
An 8085 assembler processes the program below; the instruction sizes are given in the comments. JNZ has the opcode C2H followed by a 16-bit address stored low byte first. What address does the assembler give LOOP, and which three bytes does it emit for JNZ LOOP?

        ORG  0200H
START:  MVI  A, 05H     ; 2 bytes
        LXI  H, 2050H   ; 3 bytes
LOOP:   MOV  M, A       ; 1 byte
        INX  H          ; 1 byte
        DCR  A          ; 1 byte
        JNZ  LOOP       ; 3 bytes
        HLT             ; 1 byte
questions.explanation: The location counter starts at 0200H and advances by 2 and then 3 bytes, so LOOP = 0205H; JNZ LOOP is emitted as C2H, then the low byte 05H and the high byte 02H. Counting one location per instruction would wrongly give 0202H.

questions.questionText: Why does a typical assembler make two passes over the source program?
options: Pass 1 assigns an address to every label and builds the symbol table, so that pass 2 can generate code even for forward references to labels defined later
Pass 1 checks the syntax and pass 2 optimises the code for speed
Pass 1 generates code for the host and pass 2 generates code for the target processor
Pass 1 links the library routines and pass 2 loads the program into memory
questions.explanation: An instruction such as JMP DONE may appear before DONE is defined; stepping the location counter through the whole source first gives every label an address, which pass 2 then substitutes into the machine code.

questions.questionText: Object files A.o and B.o are linked, in that order, into flash starting at 0x08000000, with B's code section placed directly after A's. A's code section is 0x1A2 bytes long, every code section must start on a 4-byte boundary, and function g is at offset 0x30 inside B's code section. What final address does the linker assign to g when it resolves A's call to g?
questions.explanation: B starts at 0x08000000 + 0x1A2 = 0x080001A2 rounded up to a multiple of 4, i.e. 0x080001A4, so g is at 0x080001A4 + 0x30 = 0x080001D4. Ignoring alignment gives 0x080001D2, and 0x08000030 is the unrelocated offset.

questions.questionText: Which statement about an instruction-set simulator (ISS) is NOT correct?
options: It lets the programmer inspect and change any register or memory location and stop anywhere, giving excellent controllability and observability
It tests the program at full speed against the product's real sensors and actuators
It runs on the development computer, so software can be tested before the target hardware exists
It usually executes the program far more slowly than the real processor would
questions.explanation: An ISS is a host program that models the target, so it is slow and has no real I/O environment; full-speed testing with the real hardware needs an emulator, on-chip debug or the target board itself.

questions.questionText: A debugger sets a software breakpoint by overwriting the instruction at the breakpoint address with a special break (trap) instruction. Why can this method not be used for code executing from mask-programmed ROM?
options: ROM is too slow to supply a break instruction within one fetch cycle
Break instructions may only be executed in supervisor mode
Code stored in ROM cannot contain branch or trap instructions
The break instruction has to be written into program memory, which ROM does not allow, so hardware breakpoint comparators that match the fetch address are used instead
questions.explanation: A software breakpoint changes memory contents, which needs writable program memory (RAM, or flash reprogrammed by the debugger); on-chip debug logic offers a few hardware breakpoints that compare the PC with set addresses without modifying the code.

questions.questionText: Which tool writes the final linked binary image into the target's EPROM or flash chip, often before the chip is fitted to the board?
questions.explanation: The device programmer (or an in-system programming interface) loads the executable image into non-volatile memory; the linker only creates the image, and the ISS only runs it on the host.

questions.questionText: An Intel HEX data record has the form :LL AAAA TT DD… CC, where LL is the byte count, AAAA the load address, TT the record type and CC the two's complement of the 8-bit sum of all bytes from LL to the last data byte. Which checksum ends the record that loads the two bytes 3EH and 05H at address 0100H (type 00)?
questions.explanation: Sum = 02H + 01H + 00H + 00H + 3EH + 05H = 46H, and its two's complement is 100H − 46H = BAH. 46H is the raw sum, B9H its one's complement, and BBH results from leaving out the address bytes.

questions.questionText: An instruction-set simulator executes 2 million target instructions per second on the host. A test program executes 600 million instructions; the real target runs at 100 MHz with an average CPI of 1.5 on this program. How long does the ISS run take, and how many times slower is it than the real target?
questions.explanation: ISS time = 600 × 10^6 / (2 × 10^6 per s) = 300 s; target time = 600 × 10^6 × 1.5 / 100 MHz = 9 s, so the ISS is 300 / 9 ≈ 33.3 times slower. Ignoring the CPI would give 6 s on the target and a ratio of 50.

questions.questionText: Many modern microcontrollers contain on-chip debug logic reached through a JTAG or SWD port. What does this provide compared with a traditional in-circuit emulator?
options: A software model of the processor on the host, so code can run before any hardware exists
Halting, breakpoints, single-stepping and register and memory access on the production chip itself through a few pins, without substituting special emulation hardware for the processor
Automatic translation of C source into optimised assembly language
A higher clock frequency during normal operation of the product
questions.explanation: The debug unit is built into every chip and driven by a cheap probe, giving most ICE features in the real circuit at full speed; a software model on the host is an ISS.

questions.questionText: Which tool combines separately compiled object files with library routines, resolves the references between them and fixes final memory addresses to produce one executable image?
questions.explanation: The linker (with a locator for embedded targets) merges object files and libraries and relocates them to their final addresses; the assembler only produces the individual object files.

questions.questionText: What does a profiler tell an embedded programmer?
options: Whether the program's syntax conforms to the C standard
The final address the linker assigned to every function
How much execution time, or how many executions, each function or loop accounts for, showing where optimisation will pay off
The exact electrical waveforms on the processor's pins
questions.explanation: Profiling measures where run time is actually spent, so optimisation effort or hardware acceleration goes to the hot spots; the linker's map file lists addresses, and a logic analyser shows waveforms.

questions.questionText: A processor clocked at 300 MHz completes 1,054,200 Dhrystone iterations per second. Taking the VAX 11/780's 1757 Dhrystones per second as 1 MIPS, what are its Dhrystone MIPS rating and its DMIPS per MHz?
questions.explanation: DMIPS = 1,054,200 / 1757 = 600, and 600 / 300 MHz = 2.0 DMIPS/MHz. Dividing by 1000 instead of 1757 would give 1054.

questions.questionText: Which benchmark suite was created by an industry consortium specifically to compare embedded processors on application-like workloads such as automotive, networking and consumer tasks?
questions.explanation: EEMBC (the Embedded Microprocessor Benchmark Consortium) publishes suites drawn from embedded application areas; Dhrystone and Whetstone are single synthetic programs, and LINPACK measures floating-point linear algebra.

questions.questionText: An embedded controller must execute 1.2 million instructions in every 20 ms frame, and the processor may be at most 70 % loaded. Four candidates implement the same instruction set, so the instruction count is the same on each. Which is the cheapest candidate that meets the requirement?
questions.explanation: Required rate = 1.2 × 10^6 / 0.02 s = 60 MIPS, and at 70 % load the processor needs 60 / 0.7 = 85.7 MIPS. A (80 MIPS) fails, and of B, C and D, C is the cheapest; ignoring the load limit would wrongly pick A.

questions.questionText: Processors A and B implement the same instruction set, and a program compiles to the same instructions for both. A runs at 100 MHz with an average CPI of 1.25 on the program; B runs at 150 MHz with an average CPI of 2.0. Which runs the program faster?
questions.explanation: A delivers 100 / 1.25 = 80 MIPS and B 150 / 2.0 = 75 MIPS; with equal instruction counts A is 80 / 75 = 1.07 times faster, so clock frequency alone does not decide performance.

questions.questionText: Which processor is the best fit for a smart-home display that runs Linux with a graphical user interface, Wi-Fi networking and downloadable applications?
options: An 8-bit microcontroller with 2 KB of on-chip SRAM
A 32- or 64-bit application processor with an MMU and external DRAM, such as a Cortex-A class core
A fixed-point DSP optimised for multiply-accumulate operations
A custom single-purpose processor designed for the display
questions.explanation: Linux with downloadable applications needs virtual memory (an MMU), a large RAM and a fast general-purpose core; small MCUs, DSPs and single-purpose hardware lack those resources or the flexibility.

subtopics.title: Application-Specific Instruction-Set Processors
subtopics.subtitle: ASIPs: microcontrollers, DSPs, network processors, and ASIC vs FPGA implementation

concepts.text: Where ASIPs Sit

An application-specific instruction-set processor (ASIP) is a programmable processor whose instruction set, datapath and peripherals are tailored to one class of applications, for example signal processing, control, graphics or packet handling. Programs are still written and loaded as software, but custom instructions (such as a single-cycle multiply-accumulate) and special functional units let the application run faster and with less power than on a general-purpose processor, while the design remains far more flexible than a custom single-purpose processor. The price is higher NRE than buying a general-purpose chip, because the ASIP and its compiler, assembler and simulator must be developed; digital signal processors, microcontrollers and graphics processing units are the common examples.
Microcontrollers
A microcontroller (MCU) is an ASIP for embedded control: a whole computer on one chip.
items: On-chip resources: CPU, program Flash, SRAM, sometimes EEPROM, plus peripherals such as timers and counters, PWM generators, ADC and DAC, UART, SPI and I2C interfaces, GPIO ports, a watchdog timer and an interrupt controller.
Instruction set tuned for control: bit set, clear and test instructions on single I/O pins, direct access to special-function registers, short branch offsets.
Low cost (from a fraction of a dollar), low power with sleep and idle modes, small packages, wide supply-voltage range and no external memory chips.
Programmed in C or assembly, often without any operating system; the reset vector starts a main loop or a small RTOS.

rows: 4 KB ROM, 128 B RAM, 4 x 8-bit ports, 2 timers, UART, 5 interrupt sources
32 KB Flash, 2 KB SRAM, 1 KB EEPROM, 16 MHz, 10-bit ADC, PWM; the Arduino Uno chip
Nested vectored interrupt controller, low-power modes, M4 adds DSP instructions and optional FPU; used in STM32, nRF, LPC
Few instructions, on-chip Flash, ADC, timers, cheap and popular for small products

concepts.text: Digital Signal Processors

A digital signal processor (DSP) is an ASIP for algorithms that operate on streams of samples: FIR and IIR filtering, FFT, correlation, audio and video codecs, modems and motor control. These algorithms are dominated by the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operation applied over long loops, so DSPs provide a hardware MAC unit that multiplies and adds in a single cycle with a wide accumulator to avoid overflow. They use a Harvard or modified Harvard architecture with several buses so that an instruction and two data operands can be fetched in one cycle, address generators with circular (modulo) addressing for delay-line buffers and bit-reversed addressing for FFT, zero-overhead hardware loops, saturating arithmetic and often VLIW or SIMD execution of several MACs per cycle.

concepts.plainText: FIR filter: y[n] = sum over k of h[k] x[n-k], one MAC per tap

concepts.text: Fixed-point versus floating-point DSPs:
items: Fixed-point (16- or 24-bit): smaller, cheaper and lower power; the programmer must scale data to avoid overflow and manage precision (e.g. Q15 format holds values in the range -1 to just under +1 with a resolution of 2^-15). Examples: TI TMS320C5000 and C2000, ADI Blackfin.
Floating-point (32-bit): wide dynamic range, easier programming and porting of algorithms, higher cost and power. Examples: TI TMS320C67x, ADI SHARC.
Many modern chips mix a general-purpose core with a DSP core or DSP instructions (ARM Cortex-M4/M7, application processors with SIMD extensions).

concepts.text: Less-General ASIPs and Implementation Choices

Beyond MCUs and DSPs there are ASIPs built for narrower domains. Network processors (Intel IXP, Cavium Octeon, Marvell) handle packet classification, forwarding, checksum and CRC computation and queue management with many small multithreaded processing engines and table-lookup hardware, at wire speed. Graphics processing units run thousands of threads in SIMD fashion for pixel and matrix work, media processors accelerate video codecs, and crypto engines implement AES and RSA. Configurable processor cores such as Tensilica Xtensa or ARC let a designer add custom instructions and generate a matching compiler automatically, which lowers the NRE that normally limits ASIP use.

concepts.text: Choosing between an MCU, a DSP and a general-purpose processor for a task:
items: Control-oriented work with many I/O pins, timers and interrupts, modest computation and tight cost or power: microcontroller.
Repetitive arithmetic on sampled data such as filtering, FFT, audio, modem or motor-current loops: DSP (or an MCU with DSP extensions if the load is light).
Large, changing software with an operating system, networking stacks, file systems and user interfaces: general-purpose 32/64-bit processor, often with an MCU or DSP alongside.
Extreme performance or power at very high volume with a fixed function: custom single-purpose hardware in an ASIC, prototyped on an FPGA.

concepts.text: IC technology is independent of processor type: any of the three processor types can be implemented in full-custom VLSI (every transistor and wire placed by hand for the best performance, size and power at the highest NRE), in semi-custom ASIC technology (gate arrays with prefabricated transistors and custom metal layers, or standard cells assembled from a library), or in a programmable logic device (PLA and PAL for small logic, FPGA for large designs) that needs no fabrication at all. An ASIP is usually bought as a fabricated chip, but a soft-core ASIP such as a configurable RISC or MicroBlaze/NIOS can also be synthesised into an FPGA next to custom hardware.
Going Deeper: Inside MCUs and DSPs

An ASIP designer starts by profiling the target applications, finds the few operations that dominate run time and turns each into a single instruction backed by its own hardware. On a general-purpose RISC one FIR tap costs about seven instructions: two loads, a multiply, an add, two pointer updates and a loop test and branch. A DSP performs the same tap with one MAC instruction whose two operand fetches and pointer updates happen in parallel in the same cycle, so both time and energy per result fall because far fewer instructions are fetched and decoded. The price is that code outside the chosen domain gains nothing, and the compiler, assembler and debugger must all understand the special instructions.

concepts.text: A Q15 number stores the fraction x as the 16-bit integer round(x × 2^15), so its range is −1 to 1 − 2^−15. Multiplying two Q15 integers gives a Q30 product in 32 bits with two sign bits; shifting it right by 15 returns a Q15 result, while DSP hardware in fractional mode shifts left by one to form Q31 and keeps the upper half. Addition needs no shift but can leave the range, so DSPs saturate, clamping to 7FFFH or 8000H instead of wrapping round to the wrong sign. The only product that overflows is −1 × −1 = +1, and a 40-bit accumulator holding 32-bit products has 8 guard bits, so sums of up to 2^8 times full scale fit before the final rounding and saturation.

DSP address generators update pointers in parallel with the arithmetic. With circular (modulo) addressing the pointer follows p ← base + ((p − base + step) mod L), so the samples of a filter delay line of length L never have to be shifted; bit-reversed addressing reverses the log2 N index bits so that radix-2 FFT results can be read out in natural order. A zero-overhead loop keeps a loop counter and the loop start and end addresses in hardware registers: when the program counter reaches the end address the sequencer jumps back and decrements the counter without executing any instruction. With a one-cycle MAC body and a three-cycle software decrement, test and branch, a 64-tap loop drops from 256 to 64 cycles.

Selecting a processor, and when to add a co-processor:
items: Start from the workload: control and I/O with modest arithmetic points to an MCU, continuous arithmetic on sampled data to a DSP (compared in MMACS), and large, changing software with an OS to a general-purpose processor.

Then check the peripheral mix, memory size, active and sleep power, unit cost, tool chain and RTOS support, and long-term availability; for battery products compare energy per task, E = P × t, not power alone.

A co-processor is a separate execution unit that the host CPU drives through special instructions or memory-mapped command registers, such as the 8087 floating-point unit beside the 8086, an AES engine or a GPU; the host keeps control of the program.
A co-processor speeds up only the fraction f of run time that it handles, so the overall gain follows Amdahl's law below.

concepts.plainText: Overall speedup S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/k), where f is the accelerated fraction of run time and k is the co-processor's speedup on that fraction

concepts.text: Common slips: a classic 8051 timer counts machine cycles (f_osc/12), not oscillator cycles; the value loaded is 2^n minus the count, not the count; AVR UBRR and CTC compare values end in −1 because the counter includes zero; a Q15 product is shifted by 15, not 16; and a bit-reversed index uses log2 N bits, so index 1 becomes 4 in an 8-point FFT but 8 in a 16-point FFT.
